docs.title: Accessing RDBMS with Spring R2DBC and Spring Data R2DBC
docs.text:
R2DBC (Reactive Relational Database Connectivity) brings non-blocking access to relational databases. Spring provides two layers on top of it: the core spring-r2dbc module (a ConnectionFactory, DatabaseClient, and R2dbcTransactionManager) and Spring Data R2DBC (R2dbcEntityTemplate, R2dbcRepository, auditing, entity callbacks).

This page follows the flow used across the chapter: generate a project as in Getting Started, add the dependency, work with the thin client first (ConnectionFactory, DatabaseClient), then move to the rich Spring Data abstractions (R2dbcEntityTemplate, R2dbcRepository).

Dedicated repository

The companion repository hantsy/spring-r2dbc-sample tracks the current R2DBC features in depth — DatabaseClient, R2dbcEntityTemplate, repositories, auditing, Postgres JSON/NOTIFY, binary data, jOOQ, Kotlin coroutines, and more. The former samples of this repository were updated from the legacy folder into the small per-feature modules listed below.

docs.title: Connection factories
docs.text:
Every R2DBC application starts with a ConnectionFactory. The R2DBC spec defines a portable way to obtain one — from a URL, from options, or from the driver's native builder:

public class PgConnectionFactories {

    static ConnectionFactory fromUrl() {
        return ConnectionFactories.get("r2dbc:postgres://user:password@localhost/test");
    }

    static ConnectionFactory fromOptions() {
        var options = ConnectionFactoryOptions.builder()
                .option(ConnectionFactoryOptions.HOST, "localhost")
                .option(ConnectionFactoryOptions.DATABASE, "test")
                .option(ConnectionFactoryOptions.USER, "user")
                .option(ConnectionFactoryOptions.PASSWORD, "password")
                .option(ConnectionFactoryOptions.DRIVER, "postgresql")
                .build();
        return ConnectionFactories.get(options);
    }

    static ConnectionFactory pgConnectionFactory() {
        return new PostgresqlConnectionFactory(
                PostgresqlConnectionConfiguration.builder()
                        .host("localhost")
                        .database("blogdb")
                        .username("user")
                        .password("password")
                        .build()
        );
    }
}

The same three patterns work for every supported driver — H2, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, MSSQL — see the r2dbc-connection-factories sample and the connection-factories module of the dedicated repository for the complete variants.

With Spring Boot, no configuration class is needed at all — set the connection in application.properties:

spring.r2dbc.url=r2dbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/blogdb
spring.r2dbc.username=user
spring.r2dbc.password=password

docs.title: Schema initialization
docs.text:
R2DBC has no schema generation. Pick one of the three approaches used across the samples:

  1. ConnectionFactoryInitializer (plain Spring applications) — run schema.sql/data.sql at startup:

    @Bean
ConnectionFactoryInitializer initializer(ConnectionFactory connectionFactory) {
    ConnectionFactoryInitializer initializer = new ConnectionFactoryInitializer();
    initializer.setConnectionFactory(connectionFactory);

    CompositeDatabasePopulator populator = new CompositeDatabasePopulator();
    populator.addPopulators(new ResourceDatabasePopulator(new ClassPathResource("schema.sql")));
    populator.addPopulators(new ResourceDatabasePopulator(new ClassPathResource("data.sql")));
    initializer.setDatabasePopulator(populator);

    return initializer;
}

  2. Spring Boot SQL init — with spring.sql.init.mode=always, Boot runs the same schema.sql/data.sql automatically.

  3. R2dbc Migrate — versioned migrations (Flyway-style) for reactive databases:

    <dependency>
  <groupId>name.nkonev.r2dbc-migrate</groupId>
  <artifactId>r2dbc-migrate-spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
  <version>4.0.1</version>
</dependency>

    r2dbc.migrate.resources-path=classpath:/db/migration/*.sql

    Migrations live in src/main/resources/db/migration/ as V1__schema.sql, V2__sample_data.sql, and so on — see the r2dbc-migrate sample.

docs.title: DatabaseClient (thin client)
docs.text:
DatabaseClient is the fluent, non-blocking SQL client — it moved into Spring core (spring-r2dbc) in 5.3 and is autoconfigured by spring-boot-starter-r2dbc. For a plain Spring application, declare it explicitly:

@Bean
DatabaseClient databaseClient(ConnectionFactory connectionFactory) {
    return DatabaseClient.builder()
            .connectionFactory(connectionFactory)
            .namedParameters(true)
            .build();
}

@Bean
ReactiveTransactionManager transactionManager(ConnectionFactory connectionFactory) {
    return new R2dbcTransactionManager(connectionFactory);
}

Queries use named parameters and a row mapping function:

public Flux<Post> findByTitleContains(String name) {
    return this.databaseClient
            .sql("SELECT * FROM posts WHERE title LIKE :title")
            .bind("title", "%" + name + "%")
            .map(MAPPING_FUNCTION)
            .all();
}

public Mono<UUID> save(Post p) {
    return this.databaseClient.sql(
                    "INSERT INTO posts (title, content, status, tags) VALUES (:title, :content, :status, :tags)")
            .filter((statement, _) -> statement.returnGeneratedValues("id").execute())
            .bindValues(
                    Map.of("title", p.title(),
                            "content", p.content(),
                            "status", p.status(),
                            "tags", p.tags().toArray(new String[0]))
            )
            .fetch()
            .first()
            .map(r -> (UUID) r.get("id"));
}

It also exposes lower-level escapes when needed — statement tuning through the filter hook:

public Flux<Post> findAll() {
    return this.databaseClient
            .sql("SELECT * FROM posts")
            .filter((statement, executeFunction) -> statement.fetchSize(10).execute())
            .map(MAPPING_FUNCTION)
            .all();
}

See the r2dbc-databaseclient sample for the complete CRUD repository built on DatabaseClient — including generated values, batch inserts through inConnectionMany(...), and transactions with TransactionalOperator.

docs.title: R2dbcEntityTemplate
docs.text:
R2dbcEntityTemplate adds entity mapping, criteria queries, and optimistic locking on top of DatabaseClient:

@Component
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class PostRepository {

    private final R2dbcEntityTemplate template;

    public Flux<Post> findByTitleContains(String name) {
        return this.template.select(Post.class)
                .matching(Query.query(where("title").like("%" + name + "%")).limit(10).offset(0))
                .all();
    }

    public Mono<Post> findById(UUID id) {
        return this.template.selectOne(Query.query(where("id").is(id)), Post.class);
    }

    public Mono<UUID> save(Post p) {
        return this.template.insert(Post.class)
                .using(p)
                .map(Post::id);
    }

    public Mono<Long> update(Post p) {
        return this.template.update(
                Query.query(where("id").is(p.id())),
                Update.update("title", p.title())
                        .set("content", p.content())
                        .set("status", p.status())
                        .set("tags", p.tags()),
                Post.class);
    }

    public Mono<Long> deleteById(UUID id) {
        return this.template.delete(Query.query(where("id").is(id)), Post.class);
    }
}

Entities map columns explicitly, and @Version enables optimistic locking:

@Table(value = "posts")
record Post(

        @Id
        @Column("id")
        UUID id,

        @Column("title")
        String title,

        @Column("content")
        String content,

        @Column("status")
        Status status,

        @Column("tags")
        List<String> tags,

        @Column("version")
        @Version
        Long version
) {
    enum Status {
        DRAFT, PENDING_MODERATION, PUBLISHED;
    }
}

For a plain Spring application, extend AbstractR2dbcConfiguration to register the template infrastructure:

@Configuration
@EnableTransactionManagement
@EnableR2dbcAuditing
public class DatabaseConfig extends AbstractR2dbcConfiguration {

    @Override
    @Bean
    public ConnectionFactory connectionFactory() {
        return new PostgresqlConnectionFactory(
                PostgresqlConnectionConfiguration.builder()
                        .host("localhost")
                        .port(5432)
                        .database("blogdb")
                        .username("user")
                        .password("password")
                        .build()
        );
    }

    @Bean
    ReactiveTransactionManager transactionManager(ConnectionFactory connectionFactory) {
        return new R2dbcTransactionManager(connectionFactory);
    }
}

See the r2dbc-entitytemplate sample.

docs.title: R2dbcRepository
docs.text:
The repository abstraction derives queries from method names, exactly like the other Spring Data modules:

public interface PostRepository extends R2dbcRepository<Post, UUID> {

    Flux<Post> findByTitleContains(String name);

    Mono<Long> countByTitleContains(String name);
}

Activate it with @EnableR2dbcRepositories on the configuration class (Spring Boot auto-configures it from the starter):

@Configuration
@EnableTransactionManagement
@EnableR2dbcRepositories
@EnableR2dbcAuditing
public class DatabaseConfig extends AbstractR2dbcConfiguration {
    // connectionFactory, transactionManager, initializer as above
}

Custom SQL goes through @Query:

interface PostRepository extends R2dbcRepository<Post, UUID> {

    @Query("SELECT * FROM posts where title like :title")
    Flux<Post> findByTitleContains(String title);
}

See the r2dbc-repository sample.

docs.title: Auditing
docs.text:
Enable auditing with @EnableR2dbcAuditing and annotate the entity fields:

@Configuration
@EnableR2dbcAuditing
class DataConfig {

    @Bean
    ReactiveAuditorAware<String> auditorAware() {
        return () -> Mono.just("test");
    }
}

@Table(value = "posts")
record Post(
        // ...

        @Column("created_at")
        @CreatedDate
        LocalDateTime createdAt,

        @Column("created_by")
        @CreatedBy
        String createdBy,

        @Column("updated_at")
        @LastModifiedDate
        LocalDateTime updatedAt,

        @Column("updated_by")
        @LastModifiedBy
        String updatedBy,

        @Column("version")
        @Version
        Long version
) {
}

In a real application, resolve the auditor from Spring Security's reactive context instead of a hard-coded value. See the r2dbc-auditing sample.

docs.title: jOOQ for complex queries
docs.text:
When derived queries are not enough, jOOQ composes type-safe SQL — including advanced constructs such as MULTISET aggregations — over the same R2DBC connection:

@Configuration
class JooqConfig {

    @Bean
    DSLContext dslContext(ConnectionFactory connectionFactory) {
        return DSL.using(
                new TransactionAwareConnectionFactoryProxy(connectionFactory),
                SQLDialect.POSTGRES
        );
    }
}

@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
class PostService {
    private final DSLContext dslContext;

    public Flux<PostSummary> findAll() {
        var p = POSTS;
        var pt = POSTS_TAGS;
        var t = HASH_TAGS;
        var c = COMMENTS;
        var sql = dslContext.select(
                        p.ID,
                        p.TITLE,
                        DSL.field("count(comments.id)", SQLDataType.BIGINT),
                        multiset(select(t.NAME)
                                .from(t)
                                .join(pt).on(t.ID.eq(pt.TAG_ID))
                                .where(pt.POST_ID.eq(p.ID))
                        ).as("tags")
                )
                .from(p.leftJoin(c).on(c.POST_ID.eq(p.ID)))
                .groupBy(p.ID)
                .orderBy(p.CREATED_AT);
        return Flux.from(sql)
                .map(r -> new PostSummary(r.value1(), r.value2(), r.value3(), r.value4().map(Record1::value1)));
    }
}

The jOOQ metamodel (POSTS, COMMENTS, ...) is generated from schema.sql by the jooq-codegen-maven plugin with a DDLDatabase, so the SQL schema stays the single source of truth. See the r2dbc-jooq sample and the jOOQ guide in the dedicated repository.

docs.title: Accessing Redis with Spring Data Redis
docs.text:
Redis is a key-value store that doubles as a lightweight message broker. Spring Data Redis provides a reactive variant of RedisConnectionFactory — ReactiveRedisConnectionFactory — which returns a ReactiveConnection, plus ReactiveRedisTemplate and reactive pub/sub support.

This page follows the flow used across the chapter: generate a project as in Getting Started, add the dependency, work with the reactive connection, then move to ReactiveRedisTemplate and messaging.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
Generate a project skeleton from Spring Initializr as described in the Getting Started chapter — choose Spring WebFlux and Spring Data Redis (Reactive) — or add the starter to an existing pom.xml:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-redis-reactive</artifactId>
</dependency>

Spring Boot auto-configures a ReactiveRedisConnectionFactory for you.

For a freestyle Spring project (no Spring Boot auto-configuration), use the plain dependencies instead — Lettuce is the required driver for reactive support:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.data</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-data-redis</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.lettuce</groupId>
    <artifactId>lettuce-core</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.apache.commons</groupId>
    <artifactId>commons-pool2</artifactId>
</dependency>

Start a Redis server with the docker-compose.yml in the repository root:

docker-compose up redis

docs.title: Spring configuration
docs.text:
For the freestyle path, create a @Configuration class to configure Redis and enable reactive support:

@Configuration
public class RedisConfig {

    @Bean
    public ReactiveRedisConnectionFactory connectionFactory() {
        return new LettuceConnectionFactory("localhost", 6379);
    }

    @Bean
    public ReactiveRedisTemplate<String, Post> reactiveRedisTemplate(ReactiveRedisConnectionFactory factory) {
        return new ReactiveRedisTemplate<String, Post>(
            factory,
            RedisSerializationContext.fromSerializer(new JacksonJsonRedisSerializer(Post.class))
        );
    }
}

LettuceConnectionFactory implements RedisConnectionFactory and ReactiveRedisConnectionFactory interfaces, when a LettuceConnectionFactory is declared, both RedisConnectionFactory and ReactiveRedisConnectionFactory are registered as Spring beans.

docs.title: Working with the reactive connection
docs.text:
@Inject ReactiveRedisConnectionFactory factory;

ReactiveRedisConnection conn = factory.getReactiveConnection();

ReactiveConnection provides some reactive methods for Redis operations.

For example, create a favorites list for posts.

conn.setCommands()
    .sAdd(
        ByteBuffer.wrap("users:user:favorites".getBytes()),
        this.posts.findAll()
            .stream()
            .map(p -> p.getId().getBytes())
            .map(ByteBuffer::wrap)
            .collect(Collectors.toList())
    )
    .log()
    .subscribe(null, null, ()-> log.info("added favorites..."));

And show my favorites in the controller.

@RestController()
@RequestMapping(value = "/favorites")
class FavoriteController {

    private final ReactiveRedisConnectionFactory factory;

    public FavoriteController(ReactiveRedisConnectionFactory factory) {
        this.factory = factory;
    }

    @GetMapping("")
    public Mono<List<String>> all() {
        return this.factory.getReactiveConnection()
                .setCommands()
                .sMembers(ByteBuffer.wrap("users:user:favorites".getBytes()))
                .map(FavoriteController::toString)
                .collectList();
    }

    private static String toString(ByteBuffer byteBuffer) {

        byte[] bytes = new byte[byteBuffer.remaining()];
        byteBuffer.get(bytes);
        return new String(bytes);
    }

}

For Spring Boot applications, the configuration can be simplified. Just add spring-boot-starter-data-redis-reactive into the project dependencies.

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-redis-reactive</artifactId>
</dependency>

Spring boot provides auto-configuration for Redis, and registers ReactiveRedisConnectionFactory for you automatically.

docs.title: ReactiveRedisTemplate
docs.text:
Beside the ReactiveRedisConnectionFactory, Spring Data Redis also provides a variant for RedisTemplate.

Let's try to add some sample via a generic Repository interface. Create a Post class to present a Redis hash data, add @RedisHash("posts") to Post class.

@Data
@ToString
@Builder
@NoArgsConstructor
@AllArgsConstructor
@RedisHash("posts")
class Post {

    @Id
    private String id;
    private String title;
    private String content;

}

Create a PostRepository and use ReactiveRedisOperations to access the Redis database.

@Repository
@RequiredArgsConstructor
class PostRepository {
    private final ReactiveRedisOperations<String, Post> reactiveRedisOperations;

    public Flux<Post> findAll(){
        return this.reactiveRedisOperations.opsForList().range("posts", 0, -1);
    }

    public Mono<Post> findById(String id) {
        return this.findAll().filter(p -> p.getId().equals(id)).last();
    }

    public Mono<Long> save(Post post){
        return this.reactiveRedisOperations.opsForList().rightPush("posts", post);
    }

    public Mono<Boolean> deleteAll() {
        return this.reactiveRedisOperations.opsForList().delete("posts");
    }
}

docs.title: Redis Messaging
docs.text:
Redis is well known as a key value database, and it is also a light-weight messaging broker.

Declare a ReactiveRedisMessageListenerContainer bean to receive messages from Redis pub/sub channels reactively:

@Bean
public ReactiveRedisMessageListenerContainer redisMessageListenerContainer(PostRepository posts, ReactiveRedisConnectionFactory connectionFactory) {
    ReactiveRedisMessageListenerContainer container = new ReactiveRedisMessageListenerContainer(connectionFactory);
    ObjectMapper objectMapper = new JsonMapper();
    container.receive(ChannelTopic.of("posts"))
        .map(p -> p.getMessage())
        .map(m -> {
            try {
                Post post = objectMapper.readValue(m, Post.class);
                post.setId(UUID.randomUUID().toString());
                return post;
            } catch (JacksonException e) {
                return null;
            }
        })
        .switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(new IllegalArgumentException()))
        .flatMap(p -> posts.save(p))
        .subscribe(c -> log.info(" count:" + c), null, () -> log.info("saving post."));
    return container;
}

The container.receive(ChannelTopic.of("posts")) call subscribes to the posts channel and returns a Flux of messages, so the processing pipeline is plain Reactor composition.

Send a message using the ReactiveRedisOperations bean:

@RestController()
@RequestMapping(value = "/posts")
@RequiredArgsConstructor
class PostController {

    //...
    @PostMapping("")
    public Mono<Long> save(@RequestBody Post post) {
        return this.reactiveRedisOperations.convertAndSend("posts", post);
    }
}

For a wider view of reactive message channels — Redis pub/sub, Spring Integration FluxMessageChannel, and Reactor Sinks side by side — see Reactive Message Channels.

docs.title: Working with the native client
docs.text:
Redis is the exception among the stores in this chapter. Unlike Cassandra's CqlSession or MongoDB's MongoClient, Spring Boot 4 does not provide a dedicated lightweight client starter for Redis, because it supports multiple Redis client libraries with fundamentally different programming models:

  • Lettuce — the default, fully non-blocking reactive client backed by Netty.
  • Jedis — a synchronous, thread-safe client often chosen for its simplicity in blocking scenarios.

Redis connectivity continues to be managed through spring-boot-starter-data-redis (blocking) and spring-boot-starter-data-redis-reactive (reactive with Lettuce), both of which configure the higher-level ReactiveRedisTemplate rather than exposing the raw driver directly.

If you need to work with the Lettuce driver directly in a reactive context, you can inject io.lettuce.core.api.reactive.RedisReactiveCommands after including spring-boot-starter-data-redis-reactive — the Redis Messaging section above shows the ReactiveRedisMessageListenerContainer for pub/sub.

docs.title: Spring Integration Java DSL
docs.text: The IntegrationFlow DSL replaces endpoint and channel beans with a fluent declaration. This page rebuilds the flow from the previous page — GET /all inbound gateway → reactive channel → WebFlux outbound gateway → GET /posts — with the DSL.

docs.title: The flow definition
docs.text:
@Configuration
@EnableIntegration
@IntegrationComponentScan
public class IntegrationDslConfig {

    @Bean
    public IntegrationFlow inboundChannelAdapterFlow() {
        return IntegrationFlow
                .from(
                        WebFlux
                                .inboundGateway("/all")
                                .requestMapping(m -> m.methods(HttpMethod.GET))
                )
                .channel(c -> c.flux("outboundReactive.input"))
                .get();
    }

    @Bean
    public IntegrationFlow outboundReactive() {
        return f -> f
                .handle(
                        WebFlux
                                .<MultiValueMap<String, String>>outboundGateway(
                                        m -> UriComponentsBuilder
                                                .fromUriString("http://localhost:8080/posts")
                                                .build()
                                                .toUri()
                                )
                                .httpMethod(HttpMethod.GET)
                                .expectedResponseType(String.class)
                );
    }
}

Reading the DSL:

  1. WebFlux.inboundGateway("/all") declares the HTTP entry point — equivalent to the WebFluxInboundEndpoint bean from the annotation-based version, including its RequestMapping.
  2. .channel(c -> c.flux("outboundReactive.input")) bridges the gateway to the second flow through a FluxMessageChannel created on the fly and named after the target flow's input channel. With the DSL there is no need to declare the FluxMessageChannel bean by hand.
  3. WebFlux.outboundGateway(...) is the DSL counterpart of WebFluxRequestExecutingMessageHandler: it executes a GET http://localhost:8080/posts through a WebClient and delivers the response payload, typed by expectedResponseType, to the flow's output.

The dependency list and the application skeleton are identical to the annotation-based sample; only the configuration class changes.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
The test is the same as the annotation-based sample — both routes return 200:

@Test
public void getAllPostsWillBeOk_viaIntegration() {
    this.rest
            .get()
            .uri("/all")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isOk();
}

docs.text: The DSL scales to real pipelines: add .filter(...), .transform(...), .split(...) between the gateway and the outbound gateway, and swap the outbound target for any messaging middleware. For channel patterns that connect Integration with Redis pub/sub and Reactor Sinks, see Reactive Message Channels.

docs.title: Reactive Streams and Spring Integration
docs.text:
Spring Integration extends the Spring programming model into messaging and enterprise integration patterns — channels, endpoints, gateways, and adapters. Since Spring Integration 5, the framework participates in the reactive world: message channels can be backed by Reactor Fluxes, inbound endpoints can serve HTTP through WebFlux, and outbound handlers are driven by WebClient.

This chapter shows how the pieces fit together, using two runnable samples:

  • WebFlux endpoints with Spring Integration — an HTTP inbound endpoint wired to a reactive channel and a reactive outbound handler, assembled with annotations.
  • Spring Integration Java DSL — the same flow assembled with the fluent IntegrationFlow DSL.
  • Reactive Message Channels — reactive message channels across the ecosystem: Spring Integration's FluxMessageChannel, Redis pub/sub, and Reactor Sinks.

docs.title: How reactive support works
docs.text:
Spring Integration introduces a reactive channel type, FluxMessageChannel, which implements both MessageChannel and Publisher<Message<?>>. Producers send messages to it through the ordinary send() contract; consumers subscribe to it as a Reactive Streams Publisher and get backpressure for free.

On the web side, two components bridge Integration to WebFlux:

  • WebFluxInboundEndpoint — receives HTTP requests, maps them to Integration messages, and writes the (possibly streamed) reply back to the response.
  • WebFluxRequestExecutingMessageHandler — the outbound counterpart; it executes HTTP requests through a WebClient and produces reactive replies.

Together they form a full reactive processing pipeline: HTTP in → message channel → HTTP out, without a blocking call anywhere.

docs.title: How the chapter's examples are structured
docs.text:
Both samples share the same skeleton — a WebFlux app serving GET /posts from an in-memory repository — and add an Integration layer on top that exposes GET /all. A request to /all travels through the Integration flow, which calls back into the same app's /posts endpoint through a WebClient, and streams the result to the caller.

GET /all ──▶ WebFluxInboundEndpoint ──▶ FluxMessageChannel ──▶ WebFluxRequestExecutingMessageHandler ──▶ GET /posts

The samples are plain Spring applications (no Spring Boot auto-configuration) built with the manual wiring from the Getting Started chapter, with one extra dependency:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.integration</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-integration-webflux</artifactId>
</dependency>

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• WebFlux endpoints with Spring Integration — annotation-based assembly.
  • Spring Integration Java DSL — the same flow with IntegrationFlow.from(...).
  • Reactive Message Channels — channel patterns across Spring Integration, Spring Data Redis, and Reactor.

docs.title: Reactive Message Channels
docs.text:
A message channel decouples producers from consumers: the producer hands off a message and does not know who processes it. In a reactive application, the channel itself is a stream — subscribers receive messages with backpressure, and multiple consumers can share the same source. This page compares three reactive channel mechanisms available in the Spring ecosystem, all exercised by the samples in this repository.

Mechanism Module Scope Best for FluxMessageChannel Spring Integration In-JVM, per application context Integration flows, HTTP in/out pipelines ReactiveRedisMessageListenerContainer Spring Data Redis Distributed (Redis pub/sub) Cross-process broadcast, lightweight messaging Sinks.Many Reactor In-JVM, per stream In-process fan-out, SSE/WebSocket feeds

docs.title: FluxMessageChannel (Spring Integration)
docs.text:
FluxMessageChannel implements both MessageChannel and Publisher<Message<?>>: producers call send(), consumers subscribe as to any Publisher. Declare it directly, or let the IntegrationFlow DSL create one:

@Bean
public MessageChannel fluxResultChannel() {
    return new FluxMessageChannel();
}

The Spring Integration chapter wires it between a WebFluxInboundEndpoint and a @ServiceActivator — a complete HTTP-to-HTTP reactive pipeline with backpressure from the HTTP response all the way back to the inbound request.

docs.title: Redis pub/sub (Spring Data Redis)
docs.text:
Redis channels work across processes: any application subscribed to the channel receives messages published by any other. Spring Data Redis exposes this through ReactiveRedisMessageListenerContainer, which returns a Flux of received messages — see Spring Data Redis — Redis Messaging for the full walkthrough:

@Bean
public ReactiveRedisMessageListenerContainer redisMessageListenerContainer(PostRepository posts, ReactiveRedisConnectionFactory connectionFactory) {
    ReactiveRedisMessageListenerContainer container = new ReactiveRedisMessageListenerContainer(connectionFactory);
    container.receive(ChannelTopic.of("posts"))
        .map(p -> p.getMessage())
        // deserialize and persist each incoming message
        .flatMap(p -> posts.save(p))
        .subscribe();
    return container;
}

// publishing side, from any process:
reactiveRedisOperations.convertAndSend("posts", post);

The subscription stays open for the lifetime of the container — a stream of messages rather than a one-shot query.

docs.title: Reactor Sinks
docs.text:
When all producers and consumers live in the same process, a Reactor Sinks.Many is the simplest channel. The SSE example and the WebSocket example both use it as a broadcast hub:

@Service
public class MessageService {

    private final Sinks.Many<Message> sinks = Sinks.many().replay().latest();

    public Flux<Message> latestMessages() {
        return sinks.asFlux();   // consumer side: subscribe from anywhere
    }

    public void send(Message m) {
        sinks.emitNext(m, EmitFailureHandler.FAIL_FAST);  // producer side
    }
}

The same pattern drives the reactive @EventListener in the Application Events sample: the listener forwards each event into a Sinks.Many so any part of the application can subscribe to the event stream as a Flux.

docs.title: Choosing between them
docs.text:
• Stay in-process and need to plug into Integration endpoints? Use FluxMessageChannel.
  • Stay in-process with a plain publisher/subscriber split? Use Sinks.Many.
  • Need messages to cross process or instance boundaries without standing up a full broker? Use Redis pub/sub.
  • Need durability, replay, and ordering guarantees at scale? Move to a real broker — Kafka or RabbitMQ — through their reactive clients (see the Spring Pulsar legacy sample for the pattern).

docs.title: WebFlux endpoints with Spring Integration
docs.text: This page assembles a reactive Integration flow with annotations: a WebFluxInboundEndpoint serves GET /all, forwards each request through a FluxMessageChannel, and a WebFluxRequestExecutingMessageHandler calls the app's own /posts endpoint through a WebClient and streams the reply back.

docs.title: Step 1: enable Integration
docs.text:
Add the dependency (see the chapter intro) and annotate a configuration class:

@Configuration
@EnableIntegration
@IntegrationComponentScan
public class IntegrationConfig {

    // endpoint beans below
}

docs.title: Step 2: declare the inbound endpoint
docs.text:
@Bean
public WebFluxInboundEndpoint jsonInboundEndpoint() {
    WebFluxInboundEndpoint endpoint = new WebFluxInboundEndpoint();
    RequestMapping requestMapping = new RequestMapping();
    requestMapping.setPathPatterns("/all");
    endpoint.setRequestMapping(requestMapping);
    endpoint.setRequestChannel(fluxResultChannel());
    return endpoint;
}

@Bean
public MessageChannel fluxResultChannel() {
    return new FluxMessageChannel();
}

The endpoint maps GET /all to Integration messages and writes the replies of fluxResultChannel to the HTTP response. Because the channel is a FluxMessageChannel, the reply can be a streamed Flux with backpressure honored end to end.

docs.title: Step 3: declare the reactive outbound handler
docs.text:
@Bean
public WebClient webClient() {
    return WebClient.builder().baseUrl("http://localhost:8080").build();
}

@ServiceActivator(inputChannel = "fluxResultChannel")
@Bean
public WebFluxRequestExecutingMessageHandler reactiveOutbound(WebClient client) {
    WebFluxRequestExecutingMessageHandler handler
            = new WebFluxRequestExecutingMessageHandler("/posts", client);
    handler.setHttpMethod(HttpMethod.GET);
    handler.setExpectedResponseType(String.class);
    return handler;
}

The @ServiceActivator subscribes the handler to the fluxResultChannel: every message that arrives on the channel triggers an HTTP GET /posts through the WebClient, and the reactive reply flows back through the inbound endpoint to the original caller.

docs.title: Step 4: verify
docs.text:
The sample's repository serves two posts from memory, and the test asserts both the plain WebFlux route and the Integration route:

@SpringJUnitConfig(classes = Application.class)
public class IntegrationTests {

    @Autowired
    HttpServer httpServer;

    @BeforeEach
    public void setup() {
        this.disposableServer = this.httpServer.bindNow();
        this.client = WebTestClient
                .bindToServer()
                .responseTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(5000))
                .baseUrl("http://localhost:" + this.port)
                .build();
    }

    @Test
    public void getAllPostsWillBeOk() {
        this.client
                .get()
                .uri("/posts")
                .exchange()
                .expectStatus().isOk();
    }

    @Test
    public void getAllPostsWillBeOk_viaIntegration() {
        this.client
                .get()
                .uri("/all")
                .exchange()
                .expectStatus().isOk();
    }
}

For the complete codes, check spring-reactive-sample/integration.

docs.text: The annotation style works, but the wiring is verbose. The Spring Integration Java DSL expresses the same flow in a few fluent lines.

docs.title: Coroutines
docs.text:
Spring WebFlux treats Kotlin coroutines as first-class citizens: a controller method can be a suspend function returning a single value, or a regular function returning Flow<T> for streams. Spring bridges to and from Reactor internally, so the reactive server stack stays unchanged.

The samples referenced here are kotlin-co and boot-kotlin-co in this repository, plus boot-kotlin-co and its SecurityWebFilter in the spring6-sandbox repository.

docs.title: Suspend methods in @RestController
docs.text:
Use suspend functions to erase the Reactor Mono/Flux wrapper types, allowing you to write code that looks synchronous while still being non-blocking.

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/")
@Validated
class PostController(private val postRepository: PostRepository) {

    @GetMapping("")
    fun findAll(): Flow<Post> = postRepository.findAll()

    @GetMapping("{id}")
    suspend fun findOne(@PathVariable id: Long): Post? =
        postRepository.findById(id) ?: throw PostNotFoundException(id)

    @GetMapping("byTitle")
    fun findByName(@RequestParam @NotBlank title: String): Flow<Post> =
        postRepository.findByTitleContains(title)

    @PostMapping("")
    suspend fun save(@RequestBody @Valid body: CreatePostCommand): Post =
        postRepository.save(Post(title = body.title, content = body.content))

    @ExceptionHandler(value = [PostNotFoundException::class])
    fun handleNotFound(ex: Exception, exchange: ServerWebExchange): ResponseEntity<Any> {
        return status(NOT_FOUND).body(ex.message)
    }
}

Notes on the style:

  • suspend fun replaces Mono<T> — the function suspends until the single result arrives.
  • Flow<Post> replaces Flux<T> for multi-value streams.
  • Nullability replaces switchIfEmpty: findById returns Post?, and the Elvis operator (?:) throws the not-found exception.
  • Validation (@Valid, @NotBlank) works the same as in Java, and @ExceptionHandler handles both validation and domain exceptions.

The kotlin-co sample of this repository shows the same pattern against MongoDB, with a ProblemDetail-based exception handler:

@ExceptionHandler(value = [PostNotFoundException::class])
suspend fun handlePostNotFoundException(e: PostNotFoundException): ProblemDetail {
    val detail = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, e.message ?: "Post was not found")
    detail.apply {
        title = "Not Found"
        type = URI.create("http://example.com/not_found")
    }
    return detail
}

Check the boot-kotlin-co sample from the spring6-sandbox repository.

docs.title: Coroutine friendly Repository
docs.text:
Spring Data provides CoroutineCrudRepository for coroutine-based data access — add kotlinx-coroutines-reactor and the store's reactive driver:

import org.springframework.data.repository.kotlin.CoroutineCrudRepository
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow

interface PostRepository : CoroutineCrudRepository<Post, Long>, CoroutineSortingRepository<Post, Long> {
    fun findByTitleContains(title: String): Flow<Post>
}

Derived query methods return Flow for collections and nullable types (or suspend) for single results — no reactive wrapper types anywhere.

docs.title: Transactions in coroutines
docs.text:
Spring's TransactionalOperator provides coroutine extensions — executeAndAwait for single results and the transactional extension for Flow:

// single-result transaction
val post = txOperator.executeAndAwait { tx: ReactiveTransaction ->
    posts.save(Post(title = "foobar", content = "content of foobar"))
}

// transactional Flow pipeline
flowOf("test 1", "test 2", "test 3")
    .onEach { posts.save(Post(title = it, content = "content of $it")) }
    .transactional(txOperator, newSingleThreadContext("MyContext"))
    .collect { log.debug("saved post: $it") }

The extensions come from org.springframework.transaction.reactive (executeAndAwait, transactional).

docs.title: CoWebFilter
docs.text:
CoWebFilter is the coroutine variant of the reactive WebFilter contract from Web Programming. Instead of returning Mono<Void>, the filter method is a suspend function, and the chain exposes a CoWebFilterChain whose filter call suspends.

The following example demonstrates a simple security check using a CoWebFilter.

import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component
import org.springframework.web.server.CoWebFilter
import org.springframework.web.server.CoWebFilterChain
import org.springframework.web.server.ServerWebExchange

@Component
class SecurityWebFilter : CoWebFilter() {
    override suspend fun filter(exchange: ServerWebExchange, chain: CoWebFilterChain) {
        if (!exchange.request.queryParams.containsKey("user")) {
            exchange.response.statusCode = HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED
        }
        return chain.filter(exchange)
    }
}

Declared as a @Component, the filter is picked up by component scanning and registered into the WebHandler chain — the same behavior as a Java WebFilter, with the method body written in sequential coroutine style.

Check the boot-kotlin-co sample from the spring6-sandbox repository.

A CoWebFilter can also handle exceptions thrown by the downstream chain — the ExceptionFilter in the boot-kotlin-co-dsl sample maps a domain exception to a 404 response, see Kotlin DSLs.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
kotlinx-coroutines-test provides runTest, and MockK provides coEvery/coVerify for suspending functions, Spring Mockk provides integration with Spring's testing framework, such as @MockkBean/@SpykBean.

The following PostControllerTest demonstrates how to test a controller with a mocked repository using runTest and MockK:

@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
@WebFluxTest(controllers = [PostController::class])
class PostControllerTest {

    @MockkBean
    private lateinit var postRepository: PostRepository

    @Autowired
    private lateinit var client: WebTestClient

    @Test
    fun `get posts by title with invalid title`() = runTest {
        coEvery { postRepository.findByTitleContains(any()) } returns
                flowOf(Post(id = 1, title = "test title", content = "test content"))

        client.get().uri("/byTitle?title=")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isBadRequest

        coVerify(exactly = 0) { postRepository.findByTitleContains(any()) }
    }

    @Test
    fun `get post that not found`() = runTest {
        val id = 1L
        coEvery { postRepository.findById(any()) } throws PostNotFoundException(id)

        client.get().uri("/$id")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isNotFound

        coVerify(exactly = 1) { postRepository.findById(any()) }
    }
}

The filter tests use the same tools — verify the SecurityWebFilter contract with WebFluxTest and runTest:

@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
@WebFluxTest(controllers = [HelloController::class])
class WebFilterTests {

    @TestConfiguration
    @Import(value = [SecurityWebFilter::class])
    class TestConfig

    @Autowired
    private lateinit var client: WebTestClient

    @Test
    fun `authentication failed with no user params`() = runTest {
        client.get().uri("/hello")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isUnauthorized
    }

    @Test
    fun `authentication passed with user params`() = runTest {
        client.get().uri("/hello?user=Hantsy")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isOk
    }
}

The test dependencies: kotlinx-coroutines-test, com.ninja-squad:springmockk, and io.kotest:kotest-assertions-core-jvm.

docs.title: Kotlin DSLs
docs.text:
Spring provides Kotlin DSLs for both halves of a WebFlux application — bean definitions and functional routes:

DSL Function Handlers Samples Beans DSL (bean definition) beans { } Reactor types (Mono/Flux) kotlin-dsl, boot-kotlin-dsl Beans DSL (bean definition) beans { } Coroutines (suspend/Flow) boot-kotlin-co-dsl Router DSL router { } (RouterFunctionDsl) Reactor types boot-kotlin-dsl Co router DSL coRouter { } (CoRouterFunctionDsl) Coroutines boot-kotlin-co-dsl

docs.title: The beans DSL
docs.text:
The Kotlin BeanDefinitionDSL (org.springframework.context.support.beans) replaces annotation configuration with functional registration.

fun beans() = beans {
    bean {
        CommandLineRunner {
            println("start data initialization...")
            val posts = ref<PostRepository>()
            posts.deleteAll()
                .thenMany<Post>(
                    posts.saveAll(
                        arrayListOf(
                            Post(null, "my first post", "content of my first post"),
                            Post(null, "my second post", "content of my second post")
                        )
                    )
                )
                .log()
                .subscribe { println("data initialization done.") }
        }
    }

    bean {
        PostRoutes(PostHandler(ref())).routes()
    }

    bean {
        val config = CorsConfiguration().apply { /* ... */ }
        val source = UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource().apply {
            registerCorsConfiguration("/**", config)
        }
        CorsWebFilter(source)
    }
}

fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    runApplication<DemoApplication>(*args) {
        addInitializers(beans())
    }
}

Reading the DSL:

  • bean { ... } registers a bean with a supplier; ref<T>() resolves another bean by type.
  • The DSL registers any bean the application needs — a CommandLineRunner for data initialization, the RouterFunction, even a CorsWebFilter.
  • With Spring Boot, apply it with addInitializers(beans()); in a plain Spring application, register it on a GenericApplicationContext

Check the kotlin-dsl sample shows that variant with RouterFunctions.toWebHandler(...). And the boot-kotlin-dsl sample shows the Spring Boot variant.

docs.title: The router DSL
docs.text:
The router { } function (RouterFunctionDsl) declares functional routes with a nesting style that reads top-down, replacing the andRoute chain from Annotation-Driven Kotlin and RouterFunctions:

class PostRoutes(private val postHandler: PostHandler) {
    fun routes() = router {
        "/posts".nest {
            GET("", postHandler::all)
            GET("/{id}", postHandler::get)
            POST("", postHandler::create)
            PUT("/{id}", postHandler::update)
            DELETE("/{id}", postHandler::delete)
        }
    }
}

The handlers here are ordinary Mono<ServerResponse> methods — the same shape as the kotlin-routes sample.

docs.title: The coroutine variant: coRouter and suspend handlers
docs.text:
The following example demonstrates the use of coRouter { } (CoRouterFunctionDsl) and coroutine handlers backed by a CoroutineCrudRepository:

class PostRoutes(private val postHandler: PostHandler) {
    fun routes() = coRouter {
        "/posts".nest {
            GET("", postHandler::all)
            GET("/{id}", postHandler::get)
            POST("", postHandler::create)
            PUT("/{id}", postHandler::update)
            DELETE("/{id}", postHandler::delete)
        }
    }
}

class PostHandler(private val posts: PostRepository) {

    suspend fun all(req: ServerRequest): ServerResponse {
        val data = this.posts.findAll()
        return ok().bodyAndAwait(data)
    }

    suspend fun create(req: ServerRequest): ServerResponse {
        val formData = req.awaitBody<Post>()
        val saved = this.posts.save(formData)
        return created(URI.create("/posts/" + saved.id)).buildAndAwait()
    }

    suspend fun get(req: ServerRequest): ServerResponse {
        val id = req.pathVariable("id")
        val post = this.posts.findById(id) ?: throw PostNotFoundException(id)
        return ok().bodyValueAndAwait(post)
    }

    suspend fun update(req: ServerRequest): ServerResponse {
        val id = req.pathVariable("id")
        val existed = this.posts.findById(id) ?: throw PostNotFoundException(id)
        val formData = req.awaitBody<Post>()

        existed.apply {
            title = formData.title
            content = formData.content
        }

        this.posts.save(existed)
        return noContent().buildAndAwait()
    }

    suspend fun delete(req: ServerRequest): ServerResponse {
        val id = req.pathVariable("id")
        this.posts.deleteById(id)
        return noContent().buildAndAwait()
    }
}

interface PostRepository : CoroutineCrudRepository<Post, String>,
    CoroutineSortingRepository<Post, String>

The suspend handlers use the coroutine request/response extensions: awaitBody, bodyAndAwait, bodyValueAndAwait, and buildAndAwait. The data initialization in the beans DSL runs inside runBlocking { ... }:

bean {
    CommandLineRunner {
        val posts = ref<PostRepository>()
        runBlocking {
            posts.deleteAll()
            posts.saveAll(arrayListOf(Post(null, "my first post", "content of my first post")))
                .collect { println("saved post: $it") }
        }
    }
}

Check the boot-kotlin-co-dsl sample.

docs.title: ExceptionFilter: a CoWebFilter for error mapping
docs.text:
The same sample registers a CoWebFilter that maps a domain exception thrown by the downstream chain to a 404 response — see Coroutines for the CoWebFilter contract:

@Component
class ExceptionFilter : CoWebFilter() {
    override suspend fun filter(exchange: ServerWebExchange, chain: CoWebFilterChain) {
        try {
            chain.filter(exchange)
        } catch (e: PostNotFoundException) {
            exchange.response.statusCode = HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND
            exchange.response.setComplete().awaitSingleOrNull()
        }
    }
}

docs.title: BeanRegistrarDsl in Spring Framework 7
docs.text:
Spring Framework 7 evolves the bean registration API into BeanRegistrarDsl — a registrar class you @Import instead of an initializer. 

class MyBeanRegistrar : BeanRegistrarDsl({
    registerBean { InMemoryPostRepository() }
    registerBean { PostHandler(bean()) }
    registerBean { Routes(bean()) }

    registerBean(
        name = "webHandler",
        backgroundInit = true,
        prototype = false,
        supplier = {
            RouterFunctions.toWebHandler(bean<Routes>().routes(), HandlerStrategies.builder().build())
        }
    )
})

@Configuration
@Import(MyBeanRegistrar::class)
class CustomConfig

registerBean(name = ..., prototype = ..., backgroundInit = ...) controls the bean metadata explicitly, and profile("foo") { ... } scopes registrations to a profile. The beans { } DSL above remains fully supported; prefer BeanRegistrarDsl for new Spring Framework 7 code.

Check the bean-registrar-kotlin-dsl sample of the spring7-sandbox repository for a complete example.

docs.title: Kotlin
docs.text:
Kotlin is a first-class citizen in the Spring ecosystem. Spring Framework provides dedicated Kotlin DSLs for bean definitions and functional routing (BeanRegistrarDsl, coRouter), Spring Data supports coroutine-based repositories (CoroutineCrudRepository), and the web layer accepts suspend functions and Flow wherever a Publisher is expected.

This chapter covers Kotlin support end to end, based on the runnable samples in this repository and the companion spring7-sandbox / spring6-sandbox repositories.

docs.title: Chapter roadmap
docs.text:
1. Annotation-Driven Kotlin and RouterFunctions — setup and the two classic programming models in Kotlin.
  2. Coroutines — suspend controllers, Flow, CoroutineCrudRepository, CoWebFilter, and testing with MockK.
  3. Kotlin DSLs — the beans DSL, router { }/coRouter { } routes, and BeanRegistrarDsl.
  4. Events, caching, and scheduling — coroutine-friendly events, caching, scheduling, and kotlinx.serialization.

docs.title: Annotation-Driven Kotlin and RouterFunctions
docs.text:
This page covers the Kotlin equivalents of the two WebFlux programming models from Getting Started and RouterFunction: annotated @RestControllers and RouterFunctions-based functional routes — both keeping the Reactor types (Mono, Flux). For the coroutine style, see Coroutines; for the Kotlin DSLs, see Kotlin DSLs.

The samples referenced here are kotlin, boot-kotlin, and kotlin-routes.

docs.title: Setting up a Kotlin WebFlux project
docs.text:
The essential dependencies (versions are managed by the Spring Boot parent):

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.jetbrains.kotlin</groupId>
    <artifactId>kotlin-stdlib</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.jetbrains.kotlin</groupId>
    <artifactId>kotlin-reflect</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.jetbrains.kotlinx</groupId>
    <artifactId>kotlinx-coroutines-reactor</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.projectreactor.kotlin</groupId>
    <artifactId>reactor-kotlin-extensions</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>tools.jackson.module</groupId>
    <artifactId>jackson-module-kotlin</artifactId>
</dependency>

The Kotlin compiler needs the allopen plugin so Spring classes and @Component-annotated classes can be proxied:

<plugin>
    <groupId>org.jetbrains.kotlin</groupId>
    <artifactId>kotlin-maven-plugin</artifactId>
    <configuration>
        <args>
            <arg>-Xjsr305=strict</arg>
        </args>
        <compilerPlugins>
            <plugin>spring</plugin>
        </compilerPlugins>
        <jvmTarget>21</jvmTarget>
    </configuration>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.jetbrains.kotlin</groupId>
            <artifactId>kotlin-maven-allopen</artifactId>
            <version>${kotlin.version}</version>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</plugin>

-Xjsr305=strict makes Spring's nullability annotations strict, so the Kotlin compiler enforces null-safety at the Spring API boundaries.

docs.title: Annotated controller
docs.text:
The kotlin sample mirrors the Java samples — annotation-driven controller, Reactor return types, Spring Data Mongo reactive repository:

@RestController
@RequestMapping(value = ["/posts"])
class PostController(val posts: PostRepository) {

    @GetMapping("")
    fun all(): Flux<Post> = this.posts.findAll()

    @PostMapping("")
    fun create(@RequestBody post: Post): Mono<Post> = this.posts.save(post)

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    fun get(@PathVariable("id") id: String): Mono<Post> = this.posts.findById(id)

    @PutMapping("/{id}")
    fun update(@PathVariable("id") id: String, @RequestBody post: Post): Mono<Post> {
        return this.posts.findById(id)
                .map { it.copy(title = post.title, content = post.content) }
                .flatMap { this.posts.save(it) }
    }

    @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
    fun delete(@PathVariable("id") id: String): Mono<Void> = this.posts.deleteById(id)
}

The idiomatic Kotlin details: val constructor injection, expression bodies, and it.copy(...) on the immutable data class instead of setters.

docs.title: RouterFunctions in Kotlin
docs.text:
The kotlin-routes sample replaces the controller with a RouterFunction bean — the Kotlin spelling of the Java RouterFunction style, using HandlerFunction references:

import org.springframework.web.reactive.function.server.HandlerFunction
import org.springframework.web.reactive.function.server.RequestPredicates.*
import org.springframework.web.reactive.function.server.RouterFunctions.route
import org.springframework.web.reactive.function.server.RouterFunction
import org.springframework.web.reactive.function.server.ServerResponse

@Configuration
@EnableWebFlux
class WebConfig {

    @Bean
    fun routes(handler: PostHandler): RouterFunction<ServerResponse> {
        return route(GET("/posts"), HandlerFunction<ServerResponse>(handler::all))
                .andRoute(POST("/posts"), HandlerFunction<ServerResponse>(handler::create))
                .andRoute(GET("/posts/{id}"), HandlerFunction<ServerResponse>(handler::get))
                .andRoute(PUT("/posts/{id}"), HandlerFunction<ServerResponse>(handler::update))
                .andRoute(DELETE("/posts/{id}"), HandlerFunction<ServerResponse>(handler::delete))
    }
}

The handlers are @Component methods returning Mono<ServerResponse>:

@Component
class PostHandler(val posts: PostRepository) {

    fun all(req: ServerRequest): Mono<ServerResponse> {
        return ok().body(this.posts.findAll(), Post::class.java)
    }

    fun create(req: ServerRequest): Mono<ServerResponse> {
        return req.bodyToMono(Post::class.java)
                .flatMap { post -> this.posts.save(post) }
                .flatMap { (id) -> created(URI.create("/posts/$id")).build() }
    }

    fun get(req: ServerRequest): Mono<ServerResponse> {
        return this.posts.findById(req.pathVariable("id"))
                .flatMap { post -> ok().body(Mono.just(post), Post::class.java) }
                .switchIfEmpty(notFound().build())
    }

    fun update(req: ServerRequest): Mono<ServerResponse> {
        return this.posts.findById(req.pathVariable("id"))
                .zipWith(req.bodyToMono(Post::class.java))
                .map { it.t1.copy(title = it.t2.title, content = it.t2.content) }
                .flatMap { this.posts.save(it) }
                .flatMap { noContent().build() }
    }
}

docs.title: Events, Caching, and Scheduling
docs.text: Spring's reactive support for application events, the caching abstraction, and task scheduling extends naturally to Kotlin coroutines. This page collects the coroutine-friendly patterns from the samples.

docs.title: Application events
docs.text:
An @EventListener supports suspend functions directly: since Spring Framework 6.1 the listener method can be declared suspend (or return Flow), and Spring bridges the coroutine completion into the event multicaster:

@Component
class GreetingListener {

    @EventListener
    suspend fun onGreetingEvent(event: Greeting) {
        log.debug("received event: {}", event)
        // ... suspend calls inside the listener body
    }
}

This mirrors the Java pattern in Application Events — publish with ApplicationEventPublisher, observe with @EventListener — with the handler body written in coroutine style.

When the surrounding contract requires a blocking method — Spring Boot lifecycle hooks such as CommandLineRunner, for example — wrap the coroutine work in runBlocking { ... }, as the boot-kotlin-co sample does for data initialization:

@Component
class DataInitializer(private val posts: PostRepository) {

    @EventListener(value = [ApplicationReadyEvent::class])
    fun init() {
        runBlocking {
            println(" print initial data...")
            posts.findAll()
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Scheduling
docs.text:
A @Scheduled method may be a suspend function that awaits a reactive pipeline with awaitSingle — from the schedule sample of the spring6-sandbox repository:

@Component
class KotlinCounter {

    private val count = AtomicInteger(0)

    @Scheduled(fixedDelay = 5)
    suspend fun scheduled(): Void {
        return Mono.defer { Mono.just(count.incrementAndGet()) }
            .doOnNext { item: Int? -> log.debug("current count:{}", item) }
            .then()
            .awaitSingle()
    }

    suspend fun getInvocationCount(): Int {
        return count.get()
    }
}

The scheduler subscribes to the coroutine completion and waits for it before scheduling the next execution — the same semantics as the Java Scheduling example, with awaitSingle() (from kotlinx.coroutines.reactor) bridging the Mono into the coroutine world.

The test asserts the counter advanced using runTest:

@SpringJUnitConfig(value = [TestConfig::class])
class KotlinCounterTest {

    @Autowired
    lateinit var counter: KotlinCounter

    @Test
    fun givenSleepBy100ms_whenGetInvocationCount_thenIsGreaterThanZero() = runTest {
        assertThat(counter.getInvocationCount()).isGreaterThan(0)
    }
}

docs.title: Caching
docs.text:
The reactive caching support added in Spring 6.1 covers Kotlin coroutines as well: @Cacheable/@CachePut/@CacheEvict apply to suspend functions and functions returning Flow, and the cache stores the completion rather than the publisher. Configure the cache manager exactly as in the Java chapter — ConcurrentMapCacheManager, async-mode CaffeineCacheManager, or RedisCacheManager — and annotate the repository or service methods:

@Cacheable(value = "posts", key = "#id")
suspend fun findById(id: UUID): Post? = ...

docs.title: JSON with kotlinx.serialization
docs.text:
Beyond Jackson, Spring Boot 4 adds a first-class starter for kotlinx.serialization: spring-boot-starter-kotlinx-serialization-json (plus its -test variant). A customizer tunes the Json instance:

@OptIn(ExperimentalSerializationApi::class)
@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class CustomConfig {

    @Bean
    fun kotlinxSerializationJsonBuilderCustomizer(): KotlinxSerializationJsonBuilderCustomizer {
        return KotlinxSerializationJsonBuilderCustomizer { builder ->
            builder.apply {
                namingStrategy = JsonNamingStrategy.SnakeCase
                prettyPrint = true
                explicitNulls = false
                encodeDefaults = true
                ignoreUnknownKeys = false
            }
        }
    }
}

Annotate the DTOs with @Serializable and Spring encodes/decodes them on the HTTP boundary. See the boot-kotlinx-serialization-json sample and the serialization guide in the spring7-sandbox repository.

docs.title: Caching
docs.text: Since Spring 6.1, the caching abstraction supports reactive return types: a @Cacheable method may return Mono or Flux, and the cache stores the completion rather than the publisher. The repository ships three samples that differ only in the CacheManager: an in-memory ConcurrentHashMap, Caffeine, and Redis. All three combine the cache with a Spring Data R2DBC backed PostRepository on PostgreSQL.

docs.title: Step 1: enable caching
docs.text:
@Configuration
@EnableCaching
public class CacheConfig implements CachingConfigurer {

    @Bean
    @Override
    public CacheManager cacheManager() {
        return new ConcurrentMapCacheManager();
    }

    @Bean
    @Override
    public KeyGenerator keyGenerator() {
        return new SimpleKeyGenerator();
    }

    @Bean
    @Override
    public CacheErrorHandler errorHandler() {
        return new SimpleCacheErrorHandler();
    }
}

docs.title: Step 2: annotate the reactive repository
docs.text:
Apply the caching annotations to the repository methods — the reactive signatures work exactly like the blocking ones:

public interface PostRepository extends R2dbcRepository<Post, UUID> {
    @Override
    @Cacheable(value = "posts", key = "#p0")
    Mono<Post> findById(UUID id);

    @Override
    @CachePut(value = "posts", key = "#result.id")
    Mono<Post> save(Post post);

    @Override
    @CacheEvict(value = "posts", key = "#p0")
    Mono<Void> deleteById(UUID id);

    @Override
    @CacheEvict(value = "posts", allEntries = true)
    Mono<Void> deleteAll();
}

docs.title: Caffeine (async cache mode)
docs.text:
Caffeine supports native async caches — enable them with setAsyncCacheMode(true):

@Bean
@Override
public CacheManager cacheManager() {
    CaffeineCacheManager cacheManager = new CaffeineCacheManager();
    cacheManager.setAsyncCacheMode(true);
    return cacheManager;
}

Add the dependency:

<dependency>
    <groupId>com.github.ben-manes.caffeine</groupId>
    <artifactId>caffeine</artifactId>
</dependency>

docs.title: Redis
docs.text:
RedisCacheManager moves the cache across process boundaries. Declare the Redis connection factory and build the manager from it:

@Configuration
@EnableCaching
public class CacheConfig implements CachingConfigurer {

    @Autowired
    private RedisConnectionFactory redisConnectionFactory;

    @Bean
    @Override
    public CacheManager cacheManager() {
        return RedisCacheManager.builder().fromConnectionFactory(redisConnectionFactory)
                .build();
    }
}

Add the dependencies:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.data</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-data-redis</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.lettuce</groupId>
    <artifactId>lettuce-core</artifactId>
</dependency>

Note

If both cacheManager and cacheResolver are set, the cache manager is ignored — configure one or the other.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
The sample test performs the same findById twice and observes the cache interceptor in the logs (the org.springframework.cache category is set to TRACE in logback.xml): the second call hits the cache instead of the database, and the eviction annotations clear the entries on save/delete.

To run the application, start PostgreSQL (and Redis for the Redis variant):

docker-compose up postgres redis
