docs.title: Application Events
docs.text:
Spring's ApplicationEventPublisher/@EventListener mechanism supports reactive return types: an @EventListener method may return Mono<Void>, and Spring subscribes to the completion.

The event sample demonstrates the pattern end to end: a publisher component publishes a Greeting event, and a listener forwards each event into a Reactor Sinks.Many so any part of the application can consume the event stream as a Flux.

docs.title: Publish events
docs.text:
public record Greeting(String message) {
}

@Component
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class GreetingPublisher {
    private final ApplicationEventPublisher applicationEventPublisher;

    public void publishGreetingEvent(String message) {
        applicationEventPublisher.publishEvent(new Greeting(message));
    }
}

docs.title: Listen reactively
docs.text:
@Component
@Slf4j
public class GreetingListener {

    public Sinks.Many<Greeting> sinks = Sinks.many().replay().latest();

    @EventListener
    public Mono<Void> onGreetingEvent(Greeting event) {
        log.debug("received event:{}", event);
        sinks.emitNext(event, Sinks.EmitFailureHandler.FAIL_FAST);
        return Mono.empty();
    }
}

The Sinks.Many bridges the Spring event mechanism to the reactive world: subscribers of listener.sinks.asFlux() receive every published event, and replay().latest() lets new subscribers catch up on the most recent event.

docs.title: Drive it
docs.text:
public static void main(String[] args) {
    var context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(Application.class);

    var publisher = context.getBean(GreetingPublisher.class);
    var listener = context.getBean(GreetingListener.class);
    listener.sinks.asFlux().subscribe(g -> log.debug("subscribed event: {}", g));

    IntStream.range(1, 100)
            .forEach(i -> {
                publisher.publishGreetingEvent("hello world #" + i + " at " + LocalDateTime.now());
                try {
                    Thread.sleep(100);
                } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                    throw new RuntimeException(e);
                }
            });
}

docs.title: Test
docs.text:
The test verifies both the Spring event and the sink, using @RecordApplicationEvents to capture events and Awaitility to bridge the asynchronous delivery:

@SpringJUnitConfig(classes = TypedGreetingEventTest.TestConfig.class)
@RecordApplicationEvents
public class TypedGreetingEventTest {

    @Autowired
    ApplicationEvents applicationEvents;

    @Autowired
    GreetingPublisher publisher;

    @Autowired
    GreetingListener listener;

    @Test
    public void testGreetingEvents() {
        publisher.publishGreetingEvent("hello world");

        Awaitility.await().atMost(Duration.ofMillis(500))
                .untilAsserted(() ->
                        assertThat(applicationEvents.stream(Greeting.class).count()).isEqualTo(1));

        Awaitility.await().atMost(Duration.ofMillis(1000))
                .untilAsserted(() ->
                        StepVerifier.create(listener.sinks.asFlux())
                                .consumeNextWith(greeting -> assertThat(greeting.message()).isEqualTo("hello world"))
                                .thenCancel()
                                .verify());
    }
}

For the complete codes, check spring-reactive-sample/event.

docs.title: Groovy
docs.text: Groovy interoperates with the Spring WebFlux stack out of the box: closures and the .& method-reference operator map naturally onto the functional routing API. The repository ships two Groovy samples, both plain Spring applications with manual wiring (see Getting Started).

docs.title: Functional routing in Groovy
docs.text:
The groovy sample builds the same blog API as the Java samples with a RouterFunction bean:

@Configuration
@EnableWebFlux
class WebConfig {

    @Bean
    RouterFunction<ServerResponse> routes(PostHandler postHandler) {
        route(GET("/posts"), postHandler.&all)
                .andRoute(POST("/posts"), postHandler.&create)
                .andRoute(GET("/posts/{id}"), postHandler.&get)
                .andRoute(PUT("/posts/{id}"), postHandler.&update)
                .andRoute(DELETE("/posts/{id}"), postHandler.&delete)
    }
}

The .& operator creates a method reference from a Groovy method, exactly where Java uses the :: operator. The handler class is an ordinary @Component with Mono<ServerResponse> methods, and the data layer reuses ReactiveMongoRepository:

@Component
class PostHandler {

    private final PostRepository posts

    Mono<ServerResponse> all(ServerRequest req) {
        ok().body(this.posts.findAll(), Post)
    }

    Mono<ServerResponse> create(ServerRequest req) {
        req.bodyToMono(Post)
                .flatMap { this.posts.save(it) }
                .flatMap { p -> created(URI.create("/posts/${p.id}")).build() }
    }

    // get / update / delete follow the same pattern
}

The application class wires the server with the standard WebHttpHandlerBuilder + ReactorHttpHandlerAdapter combination and blocks on main.

docs.title: The Groovy bean definition DSL
docs.text:
The groovy-dsl sample declares beans in a Groovy script instead of annotations. The application imports the script with @ImportResource:

@ComponentScan
@Configuration
@ImportResource("classpath:application.groovy")
class Application {
    // ...
}

And the script registers the beans in the beans { } DSL:

import com.example.demo.DataInitializer
import com.example.demo.PostHandler
import com.example.demo.PostRepository

beans {

    postHandler(PostHandler){
        posts = ref("postRepository")
    }

    dataInitializer(DataInitializer){
        posts = ref("postRepository")
    }

    postRepository(PostRepository){
        template = ref("reactiveMongoTemplate")
    }
}

ref("...") resolves another bean by name, and property assignment wires collaborators — a concise alternative to XML or annotation configuration.

docs.title: Building with Groovy
docs.text:
Both samples compile Groovy with the GMavenPlus plugin:

<plugin>
    <groupId>org.codehaus.gmavenplus</groupId>
    <artifactId>gmavenplus-plugin</artifactId>
    <executions>
        <execution>
            <goals>
                <goal>compile</goal>
            </goals>
        </execution>
    </executions>
</plugin>

For the Spring Boot variant, see boot-groovy.

docs.title: The JDK Flow API
docs.text:
The java.util.concurrent.Flow API packages the Reactive Streams interfaces inside the JDK (Flow.Publisher, Flow.Subscriber, Flow.Subscription, Flow.Processor) and adds a ready-made Flow.Publisher implementation: SubmissionPublisher.

Spring WebFlux provides adapter support for it, so a Flow.Publisher can be a controller return type or parameter.

docs.title: Flow.Publisher as a return type
docs.text:
The java9 sample returns a Flow.Publisher from a controller and bridges Reactor's Flux with JdkFlowAdapter:

@RestController
@RequestMapping(value = "/posts")
public class PostController {

    @GetMapping
    public Flow.Publisher<Post> all() {
        return JdkFlowAdapter.publisherToFlowPublisher(
                Flux.just(
                        new Post(1L, "post one", "content of post one"),
                        new Post(2L, "post two", "content of post two")
                )
        );
    }
}

Spring accepts the Flow.Publisher and drives it through the reactive request handling stack — the response is streamed exactly as with a Flux return type.

docs.title: The JDK HttpClient
docs.text:
The JDK ships a reactive java.net.http.HttpClient built on the Flow API. When you need a JDK-native client outside of Spring, it frees you from third-party HTTP client libraries:

HttpClient client = HttpClient.newBuilder()
        .version(HttpClient.Version.HTTP_2)
        .build();

HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder()
        .uri(URI.create("http://localhost:8080/posts"))
        .build();

client.sendAsync(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString())
        .thenApply(HttpResponse::body)
        .thenAccept(System.out::println)
        .join();

Inside a Spring application, prefer WebClient with the JDK connector, which wraps the same HttpClient behind the ClientHttpConnector abstraction.

For the complete codes, check spring-reactive-sample/java9.

docs.title: SmallRye Mutiny
docs.text:
SmallRye Mutiny is a Reactive Streams implementation from Red Hat, supported by Spring WebFlux since Spring Framework 5.3.10. Developers who prefer Mutiny's event-driven API can use its types directly in controllers and repositories.

Flow API based

Earlier versions of SmallRye Mutiny implemented the Reactive Streams API; current versions use the JDK Flow API instead.

docs.title: Add the dependency
docs.text:
<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>io.smallrye.reactive</groupId>
            <artifactId>mutiny-bom</artifactId>
            <version>3.1.0</version>
            <type>pom</type>
            <scope>import</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>io.smallrye.reactive</groupId>
        <artifactId>mutiny</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <!-- ... -->
</dependencies>

docs.title: Core types
docs.text:
Mutiny's two core types map directly onto Reactor's:

Mutiny Reactor Emits Uni<T> Mono<T> 0..1 item (accepts null) Multi<T> Flux<T> 0..N items

Both implement the Reactive Streams Publisher contract, so Spring adapts them automatically wherever a Publisher is accepted.

docs.title: Use Mutiny in a controller
docs.text:
Return Uni and Multi from controller methods exactly as you would return Mono and Flux:

@RestController
@RequestMapping(value = "/posts")
class PostController {

    private final PostRepository posts;

    public PostController(PostRepository posts) {
        this.posts = posts;
    }

    @GetMapping(value = "")
    public Multi<Post> all() {
        return this.posts.findAll();
    }

    @GetMapping(value = "/{id}")
    public Uni<Post> get(@PathVariable(value = "id") UUID id) {
        return this.posts.findById(id);
    }

    @PostMapping(value = "")
    public Uni<ResponseEntity<?>> create(@RequestBody Post post) {
        return this.posts.save(post).map(p -> ResponseEntity.created(URI.create("/posts/" + p.getId())).build());
    }
}

Spring handles the adaptation: a Multi is streamed like a Flux, a Uni resolves like a Mono, and Mutiny operators (onItem().transform(...), chain(...), and so on) work inside the methods.

For the complete codes, check spring-reactive-sample/smallrye-mutiny.

docs.title: Spring RestDocs
docs.text: Spring RestDocs generates accurate API documentation from tests. It integrates with WebTestClient, so every request a test performs contributes a documented snippet.

docs.title: Add the test dependencies
docs.text:
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.restdocs</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-restdocs-webtestclient</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>

The sample also wires the spring-restdocs-asciidoctor artifact into the Asciidoctor Maven plugin to assemble the snippets into a document.

docs.title: Document a request in a test
docs.text:
Register the RestDocumentationExtension, configure the client with documentationConfiguration, and add the document(...) filter to each call you want documented:

@SpringJUnitConfig(classes = Application.class)
@ActiveProfiles("test")
@ExtendWith(RestDocumentationExtension.class)
public class ApiDocumentation {

    @Autowired
    ApplicationContext context;

    WebTestClient client;

    @BeforeEach
    public void setup(RestDocumentationContextProvider restDocumentation) {
        this.client = WebTestClient
            .bindToApplicationContext(this.context)
            .configureClient()
            .baseUrl("https://api.example.com")
            .filter(documentationConfiguration(restDocumentation))
            .build();
    }

    @Test
    public void getAllPostsWillBeOk() throws Exception {
        this.client
            .get()
            .uri("/posts")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isOk()
            .expectBody().consumeWith(document("sample"));
    }
}

Running the test produces the snippets under target/generated-snippets/sample/ — httpie-request.adoc, curl-request.adoc, response-body.adoc, and friends — which the Asciidoctor build then composes into the published API reference.

For the complete codes, check spring-reactive-sample/restdocs.

docs.title: Scheduling
docs.text: Spring's @Scheduled supports reactive return types: a scheduled method may return Mono<Void> or Flux<Void>, and the scheduler subscribes to the completion. The schedule sample demonstrates a reactive scheduled task with a plain Spring application.

docs.title: Enable scheduling
docs.text:
@Configuration
@EnableAsync
@EnableScheduling
public class ScheduleConfig implements SchedulingConfigurer {

    @Override
    public void configureTasks(ScheduledTaskRegistrar taskRegistrar) {
        taskRegistrar.setScheduler(taskScheduler());
        taskRegistrar.addFixedDelayTask(
                () -> System.out.println("executing fixed delay task."),
                Duration.ofMillis(1000)
        );
    }

    @Bean(destroyMethod = "shutdown")
    public Executor taskScheduler() {
        return Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(100);
    }
}

docs.title: A reactive scheduled task
docs.text:
@Component
@Slf4j
public class ReactiveCounter {
    private final AtomicInteger count = new AtomicInteger(0);

    @Scheduled(fixedDelay = 5)
    public Mono<Void> scheduled() {
        return Mono.defer(() -> Mono.just(count.incrementAndGet()))
                .doOnNext(item -> log.debug("current count:{}", item))
                .then();
    }

    public Mono<Integer> getInvocationCount() {
        return Mono.just(this.count.get());
    }
}

The @Scheduled(fixedDelay = 5) method returns Mono<Void>: Spring subscribes on the scheduling thread and waits for completion before scheduling the next execution. Mono.defer(...) ensures the counter increments at subscription time, not assembly time.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
@SpringJUnitConfig(value = ReactiveCounterTest.TestConfig.class)
public class ReactiveCounterTest {

    @Configuration
    @ComponentScan(basePackageClasses = {ScheduleConfig.class})
    static class TestConfig {
    }

    @Autowired
    ReactiveCounter counter;

    @Test
    public void givenSleepBy100ms_whenGetInvocationCount_thenIsGreaterThanZero()
            throws InterruptedException {
        Thread.sleep(100L);
        counter.getInvocationCount()
                .as(StepVerifier::create)
                .consumeNextWith(count -> assertThat(count).isGreaterThan(0))
                .thenCancel()
                .verify();
    }
}

For the complete codes, check spring-reactive-sample/schedule.

docs.title: Configure Spring Security in Spring Boot applications
docs.text:
For Spring Boot applications, add spring-boot-starter-security to the project dependencies.

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-security</artifactId>
</dependency>

When WebFlux is detected on the classpath, the starter activates the reactive security stack automatically — HTTP Basic and form login are enabled by default, and every endpoint requires authentication.

Then add a @Configuration class to customize your security rules.

@Configuration
class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    SecurityWebFilterChain springWebFilterChain(ServerHttpSecurity http) {
        return http
            .authorizeExchange(exchange -> exchange
                .pathMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/posts/**").permitAll()
                .pathMatchers(HttpMethod.DELETE, "/posts/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
                //.pathMatchers("/users/{user}/**").access(this::currentUserMatchesPath)
                .anyExchange().authenticated())
            .build();
    }
// ...
}

See Configure Spring Security for the full configuration and the user details service.

docs.title: Configure Spring Security
docs.text:
When you are developing a Spring WebFlux application without Spring Boot, add the security dependencies from the previous page to your project.

Create a configuration class and add the @EnableWebFluxSecurity annotation to enable WebFlux support for Spring Security:

@Configuration
@EnableWebFluxSecurity
class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    SecurityWebFilterChain springWebFilterChain(ServerHttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        return http
            .authorizeExchange(exchange -> exchange
                .pathMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/posts/**").permitAll()
                .pathMatchers(HttpMethod.DELETE, "/posts/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
                //.pathMatchers("/users/{user}/**").access(this::currentUserMatchesPath)
                .anyExchange().authenticated())
            .build();
    }

    private Mono<AuthorizationDecision> currentUserMatchesPath(Mono<Authentication> authentication, AuthorizationContext context) {
        return authentication
            .map(a -> context.getVariables().get("user").equals(a.getName()))
            .map(AuthorizationDecision::new);
    }

    @Bean
    public MapReactiveUserDetailsService userDetailsRepository() {
        UserBuilder users = User.withDefaultPasswordEncoder();
        UserDetails user = users.username("user").password("password").roles("USER").build();
        UserDetails admin = users.username("admin").password("password").roles("USER", "ADMIN").build();
        return new MapReactiveUserDetailsService(user, admin);
    }
}

In the above codes:

  1. The @EnableWebFluxSecurity annotation enables Security for a spring-webflux based application.
  2. A SecurityWebFilterChain bean is required to configure the details of Spring Security. ServerHttpSecurity comes from the reactive config support — similar to the servlet-stack HttpSecurity, but it handles ServerWebExchange instead of the Servlet based WebRequest.
  3. A ReactiveUserDetailsService resolves users reactively. The in-memory MapReactiveUserDetailsService is the default choice for demos; you can customize it by implementing the interface yourself — see Customize UserDetailsRepository.
  4. The pathMatchers rules protect the API: GET /posts/** is public, DELETE /posts/** requires the ADMIN role, and every other exchange must be authenticated.

docs.title: Verify with curl
docs.text:
Start up the application and verify that the Spring Security configuration works as expected.

After it is started, try to add a new post without authentication:

#curl -v -X POST http://localhost:8080/posts -H "Content-Type:application/json" -d "{\"title\":\"My Post\",\"content\":\"content of My Post\"}"
< HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
< WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="Realm"

The server side rejects the client request and sends back a 401 error (401 Unauthorized).

Use the predefined user/password credentials to get authenticated and send the request again:

curl -v -X POST http://localhost:8080/posts -u "user:password" -H "Content-Type:application/json" -d "{\"title\":\"My Post\",\"content\":\"content of My Post\"}"
< HTTP/1.1 200 OK
< set-cookie: SESSION=b99124f7-c0a0-4507-b9be-34718af3d137; HTTPOnly
<
{"id":"59906f9d3c44060e044fb378","title":"My Post","content":"content of My Post"}

The request succeeds and returns the newly created post.

docs.title: Restricting access by path variable
docs.text:
The commented currentUserMatchesPath fragment above demonstrates a dynamic rule: it grants access only when the authenticated username matches the {user} path variable of the exchange. Wire it with .pathMatchers("/users/{user}/**").access(this::currentUserMatchesPath) to activate it.

For the complete codes, check spring-reactive-sample/security and spring-reactive-sample/security-data-mongo, which applies the same rule against a Mongo-backed user store.

docs.title: Form based authentication
docs.text:
Form based authentication is the simple approach to protect web pages.

By default, Spring Security detects the request content type and decides if it should be authenticated by a login form.

For example, there is a HomeController class.

@Controller
@Slf4j
public class HomeController {
    private final PostRepository posts;

    HomeController(PostRepository posts) {
        this.posts = posts;
    }

    @GetMapping("/")
    public String home(final Model model) {

        Flux<Post> postsAll = this.posts.findAll();
        model.addAttribute("posts", postsAll);
        return "home";
    }
}

And the content of the home template file.

<!-- /WEB-INF/templates/home.ftl -->
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
    <head>
        <title>Simple Blog Posts</title>
        <meta charset="UTF-8"/>
        <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0"/>
    </head>
    <body>
        <h1>All posts</h1>
        <div>
            <table>
                <thead>
                    <tr>
                        <th> ID</th>
                        <th>Title </th>
                        <th>Content</th>
                    </tr>
                </thead>
                <tbody>

                        <#list posts as post>
                        <tr>
                            <td>${post.id}</td>
                            <td>${post.title}</td>
                            <td>${post.content}</td>
                        </tr>
                        <#else>
                        nothing
                        </#list>

                </tbody>
            </table>

        </div>
    </body>
</html>

Add a simple configuration to protect the home page.

@Configuration
@EnableWebFluxSecurity
class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    SecurityWebFilterChain springWebFilterChain(ServerHttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        return http.authorizeExchange()
                    .anyExchange().authenticated()
//                .and()
//                    .formLogin()
                .and()
                .build();
    }
    //...
}

By default, when accessing the home URL http://localhost:8080/, the HomeController handles the request and renders the home.ftl template into an HTML page, and Spring Security invokes form based authentication to protect web pages.

By default, Spring Security provides a simple login form page. Alternatively you can customize the login form attributes or specify a new login page in the Spring Security configuration:

.formLogin(formLogin -> formLogin
        .loginPage("/login"))

Source codes: spring-reactive-sample/security-form.

docs.title: Spring Security
docs.text: This chapter explains how to secure reactive applications using Spring Security's WebFlux support. It covers authentication, authorization, and integration with reactive data stores.

docs.title: What this chapter covers
docs.text:
• Core differences between the reactive and servlet security stacks
  • Configuring ServerHttpSecurity and securing routes
  • Reactive user details services and authentication mechanisms
  • Method-level security and form-based login

docs.title: What you'll learn
docs.text:
• How to secure endpoints with declarative and programmatic approaches
  • How to configure reactive authentication providers and custom user services
  • Patterns for secure error handling and CSRF considerations in reactive apps

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Familiarity with Spring Security concepts (filters, authentication manager)
  • A working WebFlux application from the Getting Started chapter

docs.title: Chapter roadmap
docs.text:
1. An Introduction to Spring Security — how the reactive security stack differs from the servlet stack
  2. Configure Spring Security — @EnableWebFluxSecurity and ServerHttpSecurity, verified with curl
  3. Configure Spring Security in Spring Boot — the starter and auto-configuration path
  4. Method level constraints — @PreAuthorize on reactive methods
  5. Customize UserDetailsRepository — load users from a properties file or a database

docs.title: Method level constraints
docs.text: Like traditional Spring WebMvc applications, you can use a @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") annotation on your methods to prevent the execution of a method when the expression defined in @PreAuthorize evaluates to false.

docs.title: Enable method security
docs.text:
To enable method level security, add @EnableReactiveMethodSecurity to your security configuration class:

@Configuration
@EnableWebFluxSecurity
@EnableReactiveMethodSecurity
class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    SecurityWebFilterChain springWebFilterChain(ServerHttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        return http
                .csrf(ServerHttpSecurity.CsrfSpec::disable)
                .authorizeExchange(exchange -> exchange
                        .pathMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/posts/**").permitAll()
                        //.pathMatchers(HttpMethod.DELETE, "/posts/**").hasRole("ADMIN")//replace this with method level constraints
                        .anyExchange().authenticated())
                .build();
    }

    // ...
}

docs.title: Apply constraints on reactive methods
docs.text:
Annotate the methods in your business code — the sample applies the constraint on the repository:

@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")
Mono<Post> delete(Long id) {
    Post deleted = data.get(id);
    data.remove(id);
    return Mono.just(deleted);
}

@PreAuthorize works on methods returning Mono or Flux because the reactive method security interceptor checks the expression before subscribing to the returned publisher — the decision happens before any data flows.

With the URL-level rules replaced by the annotation, a DELETE /posts/{id} call from a non-admin user is rejected with 403 before the repository method runs.

For the complete codes, check spring-reactive-sample/security-method.

docs.title: An Introduction to Spring Security
docs.text:
To align with the reactive WebFlux programming model, Spring Security introduced reactive support (spring-security-web, spring-security-config). The reactive stack is no longer a separate artifact: since Spring Security 5.x the reactive classes ship inside the same core modules the servlet stack uses, so spring-security-webflux — the name you may remember from the early Spring Security 5 milestones — no longer exists.

At runtime, the reactive stack swaps every Servlet-era primitive for a reactive counterpart:

Servlet stack Reactive stack SecurityFilterChain SecurityWebFilterChain HttpSecurity ServerHttpSecurity FilterChain WebFilterChain UserDetailsService ReactiveUserDetailsService @EnableWebSecurity @EnableWebFluxSecurity ServletRequest/ServletResponse ServerWebExchange

The programming model is otherwise the same: a security filter chain intercepts exchanges, an authentication manager resolves credentials against a ReactiveUserDetailsService, and authorization rules apply per path pattern or per method.

Include the dependencies (versions are managed by spring-boot-starter-parent):

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.security</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-security-core</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.security</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-security-config</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.security</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-security-web</artifactId>
</dependency>

For Spring Boot applications, a single starter is enough — see Configure Spring Security in Spring Boot applications.

docs.title: Customize UserDetailsRepository
docs.text: The authentication manager resolves users through a ReactiveUserDetailsService, whose single method returns a Mono<UserDetails>. The in-memory MapReactiveUserDetailsService covers demos; this page shows two ways to replace it.

docs.title: Load users from a properties file
docs.text:
Spring Security provides a ReactiveUserDetailsServiceResourceFactoryBean which loads users from a properties file and creates the ReactiveUserDetailsService for your applications:

@Bean
public ReactiveUserDetailsServiceResourceFactoryBean userDetailsService() {
    return ReactiveUserDetailsServiceResourceFactoryBean
        .fromResourceLocation("classpath:users.properties");
}

The content of the users.properties file is similar to the following:

user=password,ROLE_USER
admin=password,ROLE_USER,ROLE_ADMIN

The key is the username; the value is the password and its roles.

Source codes: spring-reactive-sample/security-user-properties

docs.title: Load users from a database
docs.text:
For real applications, implement the ReactiveUserDetailsService against your user store. Using Mongo as the backend store, create a User document class that implements the Spring Security UserDetails interface:

@Data
@ToString
@Builder
@NoArgsConstructor
@AllArgsConstructor
@Document
class User implements UserDetails {

    @Id
    private String id;
    private String username;
    private String password;

    @Builder.Default()
    private boolean active = true;

    @Builder.Default()
    private List<String> roles = new ArrayList<>();

    @Override
    public Collection<? extends GrantedAuthority> getAuthorities() {
        return AuthorityUtils.createAuthorityList(roles.toArray(new String[roles.size()]));
    }

    @Override
    public boolean isAccountNonExpired() {
        return active;
    }

    @Override
    public boolean isAccountNonLocked() {
        return active;
    }

    @Override
    public boolean isCredentialsNonExpired() {
        return active;
    }

    @Override
    public boolean isEnabled() {
        return active;
    }
}

Create a UserRepository for User:

public interface UserRepository extends ReactiveMongoRepository<User, String> {

    Mono<User> findByUsername(String username);
}

Replace the in-memory user details service bean with the following, which connects to the real database:

@Bean
public ReactiveUserDetailsService userDetailsService(UserRepository users) {
    return (username) -> users.findByUsername(username).cast(UserDetails.class);
}

The security-data-mongo sample goes one step further and registers a PasswordEncoder:

@Bean
PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {
    return PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder();
}

Source codes: spring-reactive-sample/security-data-mongo.

docs.title: Header-based session id
docs.text:
By default, WebFlux resolves the session id from the SESSION cookie. Browser clients are fine with this, but API clients — mobile apps, server-to-server calls — often prefer to carry the session id in a header.

WebSessionIdResolver is the extension point that decides how a session id is resolved from a request and written back to a response. Spring ships CookieWebSessionIdResolver (the default) and HeaderWebSessionIdResolver.

docs.title: Step 1: register a custom resolver
docs.text:
@Configuration
@EnableSpringWebSession
public class SessionConfig {

    @Bean
    public ReactiveSessionRepository<?> sessionRepository() {
        return new ReactiveMapSessionRepository(new ConcurrentHashMap<>());
    }

    @Bean
    public WebSessionIdResolver headerWebSessionIdResolver() {
        HeaderWebSessionIdResolver resolver = new HeaderWebSessionIdResolver();
        resolver.setHeaderName("X-SESSION-ID");
        return resolver;
    }
}

HeaderWebSessionIdResolver reads the session id from the X-SESSION-ID request header and returns it in the same response header.

docs.title: Step 2: secure the application
docs.text:
The sample combines the header resolver with Spring Security, HTTP Basic, form login, and a session-based security context repository:

@Configuration
@EnableWebFluxSecurity
public class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    SecurityWebFilterChain springWebFilterChain(ServerHttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
       return http
               .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())
               .authorizeExchange(exchange -> exchange
                       .anyExchange().authenticated())
               .httpBasic(basic -> basic.securityContextRepository(new WebSessionServerSecurityContextRepository()))
               .formLogin(withDefaults())
               .build();
    }

    @Bean
    public MapReactiveUserDetailsService userDetailsRepository() {
        var userBuilder = User.withDefaultPasswordEncoder();
        UserDetails user = userBuilder.username("user").password("password").roles("USER").build();
        UserDetails admin = userBuilder.username("admin").password("password").roles("USER", "ADMIN").build();
        return new MapReactiveUserDetailsService(user, admin);
    }
}

A controller exposes the current session id for verification:

@RestController
public class SessionController {

    @GetMapping("/sessionId")
    public Map<String, String> sessionId(WebSession session){
        Map<String, String> map = new HashMap<>();
        map.put("id", session.getId());
        return map;
    }
}

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
1. Authenticate and request the session id:

    curl -u user:password http://localhost:8080/sessionId
# {"id":"..."}

    The response carries the X-SESSION-ID header with the same value.

  2. Call a protected endpoint with the header instead of Basic auth:

    curl -H "X-SESSION-ID: <id>" http://localhost:8080/posts

The test in the sample asserts exactly this contract:

FluxExchangeResult<Map<String, String>> result = this.rest
        .get()
        .uri("/sessionId")
        .header("Authorization", getBasicAuth())
        .exchange()
        .returnResult(new ParameterizedTypeReference<Map<String, String>>() {});

assertThat(result.getStatus()).isEqualTo(HttpStatus.OK);

List<String> sessionHeaders = result.getResponseHeaders().get("X-SESSION-ID");
assertThat(sessionHeaders.size()).isEqualTo(1);

String sessionId = result.getResponseBody().blockFirst().get("id");
assertThat(sessionHeaders.get(0)).isEqualTo(sessionId);

this.rest
        .get()
        .uri("/posts")
        .header("X-SESSION-ID", sessionId)
        .exchange()
        .expectStatus().isOk();

For the complete codes, check spring-reactive-sample/session-header.

docs.title: In-memory sessions
docs.text: The simplest ReactiveSessionRepository is a ConcurrentHashMap behind ReactiveMapSessionRepository. It demonstrates the full Spring Session setup without any external infrastructure.

docs.title: Step 1: add the dependency
docs.text:
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.session</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-session-core</artifactId>
</dependency>

docs.title: Step 2: enable Spring Web Session
docs.text:
Create a configuration class, annotate it with @EnableSpringWebSession, and declare the repository bean:

@Configuration
@EnableSpringWebSession
public class SessionConfig {

    @Bean
    public ReactiveSessionRepository<?> sessionRepository() {
        return new ReactiveMapSessionRepository(new ConcurrentHashMap<>());
    }
}

@EnableSpringWebSession installs the WebSessionManager that routes every WebSession interaction through the repository.

docs.title: Step 3: use WebSession in a controller
docs.text:
@Controller
public class SessionController {

    @PostMapping("/session")
    public String setAttribute(@ModelAttribute SessionAttributeForm sessionAttributeForm, WebSession session) {
        session.getAttributes().put(sessionAttributeForm.getAttributeName(), sessionAttributeForm.getAttributeValue());
        return "redirect:/";
    }

    @GetMapping("/")
    public String index(Model model, WebSession webSession) {
        model.addAttribute("webSession", webSession);
        return "index";
    }
}

A Thymeleaf form posts attribute name/value pairs, and the index page renders the current session's attributes:

<form class="form-inline" role="form" action="./session" method="post">
    <label for="attributeName">Attribute Name</label>
    <input id="attributeName" type="text" name="attributeName"/>
    <label for="attributeValue">Attribute Value</label>
    <input id="attributeValue" type="text" name="attributeValue"/>
    <input type="submit" value="Set Attribute"/>
</form>

<table class="table table-striped">
    <thead>
    <tr>
        <th>Attribute Name</th>
        <th>Attribute Value</th>
    </tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
    <tr th:each="attr : ${webSession.attributes}">
        <td th:text="${attr.key}"></td>
        <td th:text="${attr.value}"></td>
    </tr>
    </tbody>
</table>

docs.title: Verify
docs.text: Start the application and open http://localhost:8080. Submit the form — the attribute appears in the table, and the browser stores a SESSION cookie (not JSESSIONID).

docs.title: Test
docs.text:
The sample verifies the flow with an HtmlUnit-driven test that boots the real server:

@Test
public void createAttribute() {
    HomePage home = HomePage.go(this.driver, this.port);

    home = home.form()
            .attributeName("a")
            .attributeValue("b")
            .submit(HomePage.class);

    List<Attribute> attributes = home.attributes();
    assertThat(attributes).hasSize(1);
    Attribute row = attributes.get(0);
    assertThat(row.getAttributeName()).isEqualTo("a");
    assertThat(row.getAttributeValue()).isEqualTo("b");
}

docs.title: What's next
docs.text: The in-memory map does not survive restarts and is not shared between instances. For production, use Redis or Mongo as the session store.

docs.title: Spring Session (Reactive)
docs.text: This chapter describes session management for reactive applications. Unlike traditional servlet sessions, reactive session support uses non-blocking stores and integration points that work with the WebFlux runtime.

docs.title: WebSession: the reactive session
docs.text:
WebFlux does not use the Servlet HttpSession. Instead, every request can access a WebSession — a reactive abstraction whose attributes live on the server and whose id is exchanged with the client:

@Controller
public class SessionController {

    @PostMapping("/session")
    public String setAttribute(@ModelAttribute SessionAttributeForm sessionAttributeForm, WebSession session) {
        session.getAttributes().put(sessionAttributeForm.getAttributeName(), sessionAttributeForm.getAttributeValue());
        return "redirect:/";
    }

    @GetMapping("/")
    public String index(Model model, WebSession webSession) {
        model.addAttribute("webSession", webSession);
        return "index";
    }
}

Inject a WebSession as a controller method parameter and read or write attributes like a plain map. The session id is returned to the client in a SESSION cookie by default — there is no JSESSIONID cookie in the reactive stack.

docs.title: Spring Session for WebFlux
docs.text:
Spring Session replaces the default in-memory session store with a pluggable ReactiveSessionRepository. For WebFlux applications, activate it with @EnableSpringWebSession (and store-specific variants such as @EnableRedisWebSession or @EnableMongoWebSession) and provide a ReactiveSessionRepository bean.

Store Annotation Repository Extra dependency In-memory map @EnableSpringWebSession ReactiveMapSessionRepository spring-session-core Redis @EnableRedisWebSession ReactiveRedisSessionRepository (auto) spring-session-data-redis MongoDB @EnableMongoWebSession ReactiveMongoOperationsSessionRepository (auto) spring-session-data-mongodb

An external store is recommended for production: sessions survive restarts and are shared across instances.

docs.title: Choosing a session strategy
docs.text:
• Server-side sessions (this chapter) — simplest to reason about; pairs naturally with form login and HTTP Basic; use Redis or Mongo for clustered deployments.
  • Token strategies (JWT, OAuth2) — stateless; consider when the API is consumed by mobile apps or other services.

docs.title: Chapter roadmap
docs.text:
1. In-memory sessions — @EnableSpringWebSession with a ReactiveMapSessionRepository
  2. Redis-backed sessions — @EnableRedisWebSession with Lettuce
  3. Mongo-backed sessions — @EnableMongoWebSession with the reactive Mongo driver
  4. Header-based session id — a custom WebSessionIdResolver for API clients

Familiarity with Spring Security is helpful — the samples combine Spring Session with security configurations.

docs.title: Mongo-backed sessions
docs.text: The spring-session-data-mongodb module stores sessions in MongoDB through the reactive Mongo driver — a natural choice when your application already uses Spring Data Mongo.

docs.title: Step 1: add the dependencies
docs.text:
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.session</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-session-data-mongodb</artifactId>
    <version>3.5.7</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.data</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-data-mongodb</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.mongodb</groupId>
    <artifactId>mongodb-driver-reactivestreams</artifactId>
</dependency>

docs.title: Step 2: configure the Mongo connection
docs.text:
@Configuration
public class MongoConfig extends AbstractReactiveMongoConfiguration {

    @Value("${mongo.uri}")
    String mongoUri;

    @Override
    public MongoClient reactiveMongoClient() {
        return MongoClients.create(mongoUri);
    }

    @Override
    protected String getDatabaseName() {
        return "blog";
    }
}

With the connection property set in application.properties:

server.port=8080
mongo.uri=mongodb://localhost:27017/

Start a MongoDB server for local development:

docker-compose up mongodb

docs.title: Step 3: enable Mongo web session
docs.text:
@Configuration
@EnableMongoWebSession
public class SessionConfig {
}

@EnableMongoWebSession registers a reactive session repository backed by MongoDB automatically. The controller and template code is identical to the in-memory example.

docs.text:

docs.title: Redis-backed sessions
docs.text: The spring-session-data-redis module stores sessions in Redis through a reactive Redis connection, so sessions survive application restarts and are shared between all instances that point at the same Redis.

docs.title: Step 1: add the dependencies
docs.text:
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.session</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-session-data-redis</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.data</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-data-redis</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.lettuce</groupId>
    <artifactId>lettuce-core</artifactId>
</dependency>

Lettuce is the required driver for reactive Redis support (see Spring Data Redis).

docs.title: Step 2: configure the Redis connection factory
docs.text:
@Configuration
public class RedisConfig {

    @Bean
    public LettuceConnectionFactory redisConnectionFactory() {
        return new LettuceConnectionFactory();
    }
}

The default LettuceConnectionFactory connects to localhost:6379. To start a Redis server for local development, use the docker-compose.yml in the repository root:

docker-compose up redis

docs.title: Step 3: enable Redis web session
docs.text:
@Configuration
@EnableRedisWebSession
public class SessionConfig {
}

@EnableRedisWebSession registers a reactive session repository backed by Redis automatically — no explicit ReactiveSessionRepository bean is needed. The controller and template code is identical to the in-memory example.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Start the application and submit the attribute form at http://localhost:8080. Then inspect Redis directly:

redis-cli keys "spring:session*"

You will find the session keyed under the spring:session prefix, storing the attributes and metadata.

docs.title: Create a WebFlux application with Spring Boot
docs.text:
Spring Boot 4.x targets the latest Spring technology stack, including Spring Framework 7, Spring Security 6+, Spring Session 3+, and more.

Spring Boot added a new starter spring-boot-starter-webflux for starting a WebFlux application.

docs.title: Generate project skeleton
docs.text:
Follow the following steps to prepare the project skeleton using Spring initializr.

Open your browser and navigate to http://start.spring.io.

In the Spring Boot Initializr page, fill the following fields.

  1. Select the latest Spring Boot 4.x release (for example, 4.0.0).
  2. In the dependencies box, type reactive and choose Reactive Web to add spring-boot-starter-webflux. Optionally add Lombok, Reactive MongoDB, Reactive Redis, or other starters you need.
  3. Click Generate project (or press ALT+ENTER) to download a ZIP archive containing the project skeleton.

Download the archive and extract it to your disk, then import the source codes into your IDE.

Open the pom.xml, you will see the spring-boot-starter-webflux is added into dependencies.

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-webflux</artifactId>
</dependency>

And a spring-boot-maven-plugin is added in the initial pom.xml.

Spring Boot starter spring-boot-starter-webflux will handle the spring-webflux related dependencies and enable WebFlux support automatically. It also add logback as default logging handler.

Compare to the former vanilla version,

  1. No need explicit WebConfig, Spring Boot configures it automatically.
  2. The former bootstraping class or AppInitializer is no use now, the Spring Boot built-in @SpringBootApplication annotated class hands over the applicationContext lifecyle and application bootstrap.
@SpringBootApplication
public class DemoApplication {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(DemoApplication.class, args);
    }
}

By default, Spring Boot will use Reactor Netty as runtime to run a WebFlux application. No need extra configuration for it.

To start the application in your terminal, run the following command in the project root folder.

mvn spring-boot:run

Alternatively, to start Spring Boot applications in your IDEs, run it just like running a general-purpose Java application.

docs.text:

By default, when spring-boot-starter-webflux is included in the classpath, it uses Netty as the embedded server to serve HTTP requests.

<dependency>

    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-webflux</artifactId>
     <exclusions>
        <exclusion>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-reactor-netty</artifactId>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        </exclusion>
    </exclusions>
</dependency>

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-tomcat</artifactId>
</dependency>

The boot-start sample provides Maven profiles to switch between Reactor Netty (default), Tomcat, Jetty, and Undertow — activate one with mvn spring-boot:run -Ptomcat.

docs.title: Create a WebFlux application from Scratch
docs.text:
A working example is worth a thousand words. Let's write code and explore the reactive programming features introduced in Spring Framework 7.

As an example, I will reuse the same concept in my former Spring Boot sample codes which is a simple blog application.

Note

In this post, we prepare the codes manually and do not use Spring Boot autoconfiguration. I think it will help you to understand the essential configuration in a Spring WebFlux application.

In the following steps we will start with creating RESTful APIs for Post.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before writing some real codes, make sure you have installed the essential software:

  • Java 21. Install a JDK from Eclipse Temurin, Oracle, or your preferred vendor.
  • Apache Maven or Gradle
  • Your favorite IDE:
    • IntelliJ IDEA (Community or Ultimate Edition)
    • Eclipse IDE — with Spring Tools for Spring support
    • Apache NetBeans IDE
    • VS Code with the Java and Spring Boot extensions

Note

Do not forget to add path which includes java and mvn command into your system environment variable PATH .

docs.title: Generate project skeleton
docs.text:
Personally I prefer to use Apache Maven to build Java applications.

Run the following command to create a general web application from the existing Maven archetype.

$ mvn archetype:generate -DgroupId=com.example \
    -DartifactId=demo \
    -DarchetypeArtifactId=maven-archetype-webapp \

Note

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
The project skeleton is ready, now let's add some codes to play reactive programming.

Create a new class named Post, it includes three fields: id, title, content.

@Data
@ToString
@Builder
@NoArgsConstructor
@AllArgsConstructor
class Post {

    private Long id;
    private String title;
    private String content;

}

In the above codes, @Data, @ToString, @Builder, @NoArgsConstructor, @AllArgsConstructor are from the Lombok project.

When you compile Post, it will utilize Java compiler built-in Annotation Processing Tooling feature to add extra facilities into the final compiled classes, including:

  1. Getters and setters of the three fields, and overrides equals and hashCode methods.
  2. Overrides toString method.
  3. A builder class for creating the Post instance more easily.
  4. A constructor with no arguments.
  5. A constructor with all fields as arguments.

Create a dummy repository named PostRepository to retrieve posts from and save them back to a repository.

@Component
class PostRepository {

    private static final Map<Long, Post> DATA = new HashMap<>();
    private static long ID_COUNTER = 1L;

    static {
        Arrays.asList("First Post", "Second Post")
            .stream()
            .forEach((java.lang.String title) -> {
                long id = ID_COUNTER++;
                DATA.put(Long.valueOf(id), Post.builder().id(id).title(title).content("content of " + title).build());
            }
            );
    }

    Flux<Post> findAll() {
        return Flux.fromIterable(DATA.values());
    }

    Mono<Post> findById(Long id) {
        return Mono.just(DATA.get(id));
    }

    Mono<Post> createPost(Post post) {
        long id = ID_COUNTER++;
        post.setId(id);
        DATA.put(id, post);
        return Mono.just(post);
    }

}

Currently we have not connected to any database, so this repository uses a Map backed data store instead. When we discuss the reactive features provided by the Spring Data projects, we will replace it with a real Spring Data reactive implementation.

If you have used Spring Data before, you will find these APIs are every similar with Repository interface provided in Spring Data.

The main difference is in the current Repository class all methods return a Flux or Mono.

Flux and Mono are from Reactor, which powers the reactive support in Spring Framework 7 by default.

  • Flux represents a stream of 0..N elements.
  • Mono represents an asynchronous 0..1 result.

Create a controller class named PostController to expose RESTful APIs for the Post entity.

@RestController
@RequestMapping(value = "/posts")
class PostController {

    private final PostRepository posts;

    public PostController(PostRepository posts) {
        this.posts = posts;
    }

    @GetMapping(value = "")
    public Flux<Post> all() {
        return this.posts.findAll();
    }

    @GetMapping(value = "/{id}")
    public Mono<Post> get(@PathVariable(value = "id") Long id) {
        return this.posts.findById(id);
    }

    @PostMapping(value = "")
    public Mono<Post> create(Post post) {
        return this.posts.createPost(post);
    }

}

If you have some experience in Spring WebMvc, you will see the above codes are almost same as the existing one, except we return a Flux or Mono as the response body.

Next, create a @Configuration class and add an @EnableWebFlux annotation to activate WebFlux support in this application.

@Configuration
@ComponentScan
@EnableWebFlux
class WebConfig {

}

The application code is ready. Let's bootstrap the application.

docs.title: Bootstrap
docs.text:
According to the official documentation (see the Web on Reactive Stack section), Spring Framework 7 provides several options to bootstrap a reactive web application: https://docs.spring.io/spring-framework/docs/current/reference/html/web-reactive.html#spring-webflux

Quote

Spring WebFlux is supported on Tomcat, Jetty, Servlet 3.1+ containers, as well as on non-Servlet runtimes such as Netty and Undertow.

Every bootstrap variant follows the same three steps, built on a handful of core Spring types (Javadoc links):

  1. Build an HttpHandler from the ApplicationContext with WebHttpHandlerBuilder — the low-level contract for reactive request handling.
  2. Wrap it in a server-specific adapter: TomcatHttpHandlerAdapter, JettyCoreHttpHandlerAdapter, ReactorHttpHandlerAdapter, or UndertowHttpHandlerAdapter. Above the adapter, the WebHandler chain assembles the filters and exception handlers — see An introduction to Reactive Web.
  3. Start the embedded server.

docs.title: Apache Tomcat
docs.text:
Create a general-purpose Application class to start the application manually.

@Configuration
@ComponentScan
@PropertySource(value = "classpath:application.properties", ignoreResourceNotFound = true)
public class Application {

    @Value("${server.port:8080}")
    private int port = 8080;

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        ApplicationContext context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(Application.class);  // (1)

        Tomcat tomcatServer = context.getBean(Tomcat.class);
        tomcatServer.start();

        System.out.println("Tomcat server is running at port:"
                           + tomcatServer.getConnector().getLocalPort());
        //System.in.read();
    }

    @Bean
    @Profile("default")
    public Tomcat embeddedTomcatServer(ApplicationContext context) {
        HttpHandler handler = WebHttpHandlerBuilder.applicationContext(context).build();

        Servlet servlet = new TomcatHttpHandlerAdapter(handler);
        Tomcat tomcat = new Tomcat();

        File base = new File(System.getProperty("java.io.tmpdir"));
        Context rootContext = tomcat.addContext("", base.getAbsolutePath());
        Tomcat.addServlet(rootContext, "main", servlet).setAsyncSupported(true);
        rootContext.addServletMappingDecoded("/", "main");

        tomcat.setHostname("localhost");
        tomcat.setPort(this.port);
        tomcat.setBaseDir(System.getProperty("java.io.tmpdir"));

        return tomcat;
    }

}

The above codes perform some tasks.

  1. Create a HttpHandler from ApplicationContext.
  2. Use TomcatHttpHandlerAdapter to bridge the Servlet APIs to the reactive based HttpHandler.
  3. Start tomcat server.

Do not forget add the tomcat-embed-core to project dependencies.

 <dependency>
    <groupId>org.apache.tomcat.embed</groupId>
    <artifactId>tomcat-embed-core</artifactId>
</dependency>

You can simply run this class in IDEs as java applications.

If you want to package all dependencies into one jar and run the application in command line, eg. java -jar filename, maven-assembly-plugin can help this purpose.

Add maven-assembly-plugin configuration into the pom.xml file.

<!-- Maven Assembly Plugin -->
<plugin>
    <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
    <artifactId>maven-assembly-plugin</artifactId>
    <configuration>
        <descriptorRefs>
            <descriptorRef>jar-with-dependencies</descriptorRef>
        </descriptorRefs>
        <!-- MainClass in mainfest make a executable jar -->
        <archive>
            <manifest>
                <mainClass>com.example.demo.Application</mainClass>
            </manifest>
        </archive>

    </configuration>
    <executions>
        <execution>
            <id>make-assembly</id>
            <phase>package</phase> <!-- bind to the packaging phase -->
            <goals>
                <goal>single</goal>
            </goals>
        </execution>
    </executions>
</plugin>

mvn package

When it is done, switch to the target folder, besides the general jar, you will find an extra fat jar was generated, which filename is ended with jar-with-dependencies.jar.

spring-reactive-sample-vanilla-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT-jar-with-dependencies.jar
spring-reactive-sample-vanilla-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT.jar

Run the following command to run this application.

java -jar target/spring-reactive-sample-vanilla-0.0.1-SNAPSHOT-jar-with-dependencies.jar

When it is started, let's try to verify if it works.

#curl http://localhost:8080/posts
[{"id":1,"title":"First Post","content":"content of First Post"},{"id":2,"title":"Second Post","content":"content of Second Post"}]

docs.title: Eclipse Jetty
docs.text:
To use a Jetty server instead, replace the Application class with the following:

@Configuration
@ComponentScan
@PropertySource(value = "classpath:application.properties", ignoreResourceNotFound = true)
public class Application {

    @Value("${server.port:8080}")
    private int port = 8080;

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        ApplicationContext context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(Application.class);
        Server server = context.getBean(Server.class);

        // 4. Starts up application
        server.start();

        System.out.println("Press ENTER to exit.");
        System.in.read();
    }

    @Bean
    public Server jettyServer(ApplicationContext context) throws Exception {
        // 1. Initialize the adapter with Spring's HttpHandler
        HttpHandler httpHandler = WebHttpHandlerBuilder.applicationContext(context).build();
        // 2. Create the Jetty Core adapter
        JettyCoreHttpHandlerAdapter adapter = new JettyCoreHttpHandlerAdapter(httpHandler);

        // 3. Set up the Jetty 12 Core Path Mappings
        PathMappingsHandler pathMappingsHandler = new PathMappingsHandler();

        // CRITICAL JETTY 12 CHANGE: Bind your adapter explicitly via PathSpec
        // Use "/*" to ensure all sub-paths underneath the root context are matched correctly
        pathMappingsHandler.addMapping(PathSpec.from("/*"), adapter);

        // 4. Initialize server and attach the mapping handler
        Server server = new Server();
        server.setHandler(pathMappingsHandler);

        // 5. Setup Network Connector
        ServerConnector connector = new ServerConnector(server);
        connector.setPort(port);
        server.addConnector(connector);

        return server;
    }

}

Since Jetty 11, the Jetty artifact IDs changed: the servlet support moved into environment-specific modules such as jetty-ee11-servlet (Jetty 12, EE 11 environment), and the servlet-era ServletContextHandler bootstrap is replaced by Jetty Core's PathMappingsHandler. Declare a BOM for the EE 11 environment and use the new coordinates:

<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.eclipse.jetty.ee11</groupId>
            <artifactId>jetty-ee11-bom</artifactId>
            <version>${jetty.version}</version>
            <type>pom</type>
            <scope>import</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.eclipse.jetty</groupId>
        <artifactId>jetty-server</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.eclipse.jetty.ee11</groupId>
        <artifactId>jetty-ee11-servlet</artifactId>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

Similarly, you can run the application directly in your IDEs.

For the complete codes, check spring-reactive-sample/vanilla-jetty.

Alternatively, you can run the application in Reactor Netty, or JBoss Undertow.

docs.title: Reactor Netty
docs.text:
For Reactor Netty, replace the Application class with:

@Configuration
@ComponentScan
@PropertySource(value = "classpath:application.properties", ignoreResourceNotFound = true)
public class Application {

    @Value("${server.port:8080}")
    private int port = 8080;

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        try (AnnotationConfigApplicationContext context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(
                Application.class)) {
            context.getBean(HttpServer.class)
                    .bindUntilJavaShutdown(Duration.ofSeconds(60), null);
        }
    }

    @Bean
    public HttpServer httpServer(ApplicationContext context) {
        HttpHandler handler = WebHttpHandlerBuilder.applicationContext(context).build();
        ReactorHttpHandlerAdapter adapter = new ReactorHttpHandlerAdapter(handler);
        return  HttpServer.create()
                .host("localhost")
                .port(this.port)
                .handle(adapter);
    }

}

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.projectreactor.netty</groupId>

docs.title: Standalone Servlet Container
docs.text:
If you prefer traditional web applications and want to package a WAR to deploy into a servlet container, Spring Framework 7 provides AbstractReactiveWebInitializer to help initialize a reactive web application in a Servlet environment. This class implements WebApplicationInitializer and is discovered by the servlet container at startup.

Create a AppInitializer instead of the Application class.

public class AppInitializer extends AbstractReactiveWebInitializer {

    @Override
    protected Class<?>[] getConfigClasses() {
        return new Class[]{
                AppConfig.class,
                WebConfig.class
        };
    }
}

Note

The former AbstractAnnotationConfigDispatcherHandlerInitializer is problematic, check notes I added in the sample codes spring-reactive-sample/war

Next change the project packaging from jar to war in pom.xml.

<packaging>war</packaging>

And add the Jakarta Servlet API to your project dependencies.

<dependency>
    <groupId>jakarta.servlet</groupId>
    <artifactId>jakarta.servlet-api</artifactId>
    <scope>provided</scope>
</dependency>

Now you can run this application on an IDE managed Servlet container directly.

Or package the project into a war format and deploy it into a Servlet based container (Tomcat, Jetty) manually.

Alternatively, if you want to run this application via mvn commands in the development stage, the Jetty EE 11 Maven plugin serves the WAR in place:

<plugin>
    <groupId>org.eclipse.jetty.ee11</groupId>

    <configuration>
        <scanIntervalSeconds>10</scanIntervalSeconds>
        <webApp>
            <contextPath>/</contextPath>
        </webApp>
    </configuration>

mvn jetty:run

<plugin>
    <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
    <artifactId>maven-war-plugin</artifactId>
    <configuration>
        <failOnMissingWebXml>false</failOnMissingWebXml>
    </configuration>
</plugin>
<plugin>
    <groupId>org.codehaus.cargo</groupId>
    <artifactId>cargo-maven3-plugin</artifactId>
    <configuration>
        <container>
            <containerId>tomcat10x</containerId>
            <type>embedded</type>

        <configuration>
            <properties>
                <cargo.servlet.port>8080</cargo.servlet.port>
                <cargo.logging>high</cargo.logging>

        </configuration>

mvn verify cargo:run

docs.title: Alternative Bean Registration
docs.text:
In the example above we use ApplicationContext component scanning. For classes that are not part of the component scan, Spring Framework 7 provides a concise registerBean API to programmatically register instances as Spring beans in the ApplicationContext.

public class Application {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        AnnotationConfigApplicationContext context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext();
        PostRepository posts = new PostRepository();
        PostHandler postHandler = new PostHandler(posts);
        Routes routesBean = new Routes(postHandler);

        context.registerBean(PostRepository.class, () -> posts);
        context.registerBean(PostHandler.class, () -> postHandler);
        context.registerBean(Routes.class, () -> routesBean);
        context.registerBean(WebHandler.class, () -> RouterFunctions.toWebHandler(routesBean.routes(), HandlerStrategies.builder().build()));
        context.refresh();

        nettyServer(context).onDispose().block();
    }

    public static DisposableServer nettyServer(ApplicationContext context) {
        HttpHandler handler = WebHttpHandlerBuilder.applicationContext(context).build();
        ReactorHttpHandlerAdapter adapter = new ReactorHttpHandlerAdapter(handler);
        HttpServer httpServer = HttpServer.create().host("localhost").port(8080);
        return httpServer.handle(adapter).bindNow();
    }

}

For the complete codes, check spring-reactive-sample/register-bean.

docs.title: Reactive Streams and Spring WebFlux
docs.text:
Spring WebFlux is the reactive web framework of Spring Framework. It embraces asynchronous, non-blocking I/O and the Reactive Streams specification to build scalable, resource-efficient applications for modern cloud and microservice environments.

This page introduces the Reactive Streams specification and its implementations (Project Reactor, RxJava 3, SmallRye Mutiny, and the Java Flow API), and shows how Spring WebFlux uses them. Everything is demonstrated with short code fragments that you can run with a plain Java main method — no server required.

Audience and scope

This page is for developers new to reactive programming who want to understand the building blocks before writing a WebFlux application. For the application itself, continue to Create a WebFlux application from scratch or Create a WebFlux application with Spring Boot.

docs.title: Reactive Streams: the specification
docs.text:
Reactive Streams — official site reactive-streams.org — is an initiative to provide a standard for asynchronous stream processing with non-blocking backpressure. It encompasses efforts aimed at runtime environments (JVM and JavaScript) as well as network protocols.

The JVM specification is a small set of four interfaces, defined in the org.reactivestreams package:

  • Publisher<T> — produces a potentially unbounded number of sequenced elements, publishing them according to the demand received from its Subscriber(s).
  • Subscriber<T> — receives the signals produced by a Publisher: onSubscribe, then zero or more onNext, and finally onComplete or onError.
  • Subscription — represents the one-to-one lifecycle between a Subscriber and a Publisher. It carries the demand signal (request(long n)) and cancel().
  • Processor<T, R> — a processing stage that is both a Subscriber and a Publisher, obeying the contracts of both.

The interfaces are intentionally tiny:

public interface Publisher<T> {
    void subscribe(Subscriber<? super T> s);
}

public interface Subscriber<T> {
    void onSubscribe(Subscription s);
    void onNext(T t);
    void onError(Throwable t);
    void onComplete();
}

public interface Subscription {
    void request(long n);
    void cancel();
}

public interface Processor<T, R> extends Subscriber<T>, Publisher<R> {
}

Nothing is delivered until the Subscriber signals demand. This is the essence of backpressure: the consumer controls the flow of data, so a fast producer cannot overwhelm a slow consumer.

docs.title: A minimal Publisher and Subscriber
docs.text:
The following fragment wires a simple Publisher to a Subscriber by hand. It demonstrates the full signal protocol — no reactive library required, only the org.reactivestreams interfaces:

// A Publisher that emits 1, 2, 3 and completes.
Publisher<Integer> publisher = subscriber ->
        subscriber.onSubscribe(new Subscription() {
            private int value = 1;

            @Override
            public void request(long n) {
                for (long i = 0; i < n && value <= 3; i++) {
                    subscriber.onNext(value++);
                }
                if (value > 3) {
                    subscriber.onComplete();
                }
            }

            @Override
            public void cancel() {
            }
        });

publisher.subscribe(new Subscriber<Integer>() {
    @Override
    public void onSubscribe(Subscription s) {
        s.request(3); // signal demand explicitly
    }

    @Override
    public void onNext(Integer item) {
        System.out.println("received: " + item);
    }

    @Override
    public void onError(Throwable t) {
        System.err.println("error: " + t);
    }

    @Override
    public void onComplete() {
        System.out.println("done");
    }
});

Running it prints:

received: 1
received: 2
received: 3
done

In practice you never assemble these interfaces by hand — a reactive library such as Project Reactor does it for you — but the protocol explains what happens behind every Flux and Mono you will use in WebFlux.

Implementations are validated by a conformance test kit (the Reactive Streams TCK), which guarantees the interoperability of any compliant library.

docs.title: Project Reactor
docs.text:
The Reactor project works closely with the Spring team, and Reactor is the reactive library that Spring WebFlux uses by default. Useful entry points: the reference documentation and the API Javadoc for Flux and Mono.

Reactor provides two types that implement org.reactivestreams.Publisher:

  • Flux<T> — a Publisher that emits 0 to N elements, and then completes either successfully or with an error.
  • Mono<T> — a Publisher that emits at most one item via onNext and then terminates with an onComplete signal (a successful Mono, with or without a value), or emits only a single onError signal (a failed Mono).
Concept Reactor Analogy 0..1 result, maybe asynchronous Mono<T> CompletableFuture<T> / Optional<T> 0..N results, streamed Flux<T> Stream<T> / Iterable<T>

docs.title: Creating a Flux and a Mono
docs.text:
Add Reactor to your project (the coordinates are managed by spring-boot-starter-parent):

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.projectreactor</groupId>
    <artifactId>reactor-core</artifactId>
</dependency>

The most common factory methods are static:

Flux<String> flux = Flux.just("a", "b", "c");          // fixed data
Flux<Long> interval = Flux.interval(Duration.ofSeconds(1)); // ticks every second
Flux<Integer> generated = Flux.range(1, 5);            // 1..5

Mono<String> mono = Mono.just("hello");                // single value
Mono<String> empty = Mono.empty();                     // completes without a value
Mono<String> fromCallable = Mono.fromCallable(() -> expensiveBlockingCall()); // lazily wrap blocking code

docs.title: Subscribing: nothing happens until you subscribe
docs.text:
Reactive types are lazy by default. Assembling operators builds a pipeline; subscribing executes it:

Flux.just("a", "b", "c")
    .map(String::toUpperCase)
    .subscribe(
        data -> System.out.println("onNext: " + data),
        err -> System.err.println("onError: " + err),
        () -> System.out.println("onComplete")
    );

Output:

onNext: A
onNext: B
onNext: C
onComplete

Common pitfall

A Flux or Mono that is never subscribed emits nothing. Inside a WebFlux @RestController you return the reactive type and Spring subscribes for you; in plain Java code you must call subscribe() (or a blocking method such as block()) yourself.

docs.title: Transforming and combining streams
docs.text:
The operator style reads like the Java Stream API, but the operations are asynchronous:

Flux.just(1, 2, 3)
    .map(i -> i * 10)                 // transform each element
    .filter(i -> i > 10)              // keep elements matching a predicate
    .flatMap(i -> fetchRelated(i))    // 1-to-N async transformation
    .concatWith(Flux.just(100))       // append another stream
    .take(2)                          // only the first 2 elements
    .subscribe(System.out::println);

Combine several streams with zip — this pattern appears throughout the sample repository, for example to pace a data stream with a timer:

Flux.zip(Flux.interval(Duration.ofSeconds(1)), Flux.just("a", "b", "c"))
    .map(Tuple2::getT2)
    .subscribe(System.out::println);
// prints "a", then "b", then "c" — one per second

docs.title: Backpressure: demand in action
docs.text:
Reactor manages demand for you, and exposes it when you want to control it explicitly:

Flux.range(1, 100)
    .subscribe(new BaseSubscriber<Integer>() {
        @Override
        protected void hookOnSubscribe(Subscription subscription) {
            request(1); // ask for one item at a time
        }

        @Override
        protected void hookOnNext(Integer value) {
            System.out.println("received: " + value);
            request(1);
        }

        @Override
        protected void hookOnComplete() {
            System.out.println("done");
        }
    });

Operators such as limitRate, buffer, and onBackpressureDrop reshape demand when the default behavior does not fit.

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
Errors are signals, not exceptions thrown at the caller:

Flux.just("a", "b")
    .map(s -> { if (s.equals("b")) throw new IllegalStateException("boom"); return s; })
    .onErrorResume(e -> Flux.just("fallback"))
    .subscribe(System.out::println);
// prints: a, fallback

For tests, reactor-test provides StepVerifier, which verifies the exact sequence of signals:

StepVerifier.create(Flux.just("a", "b"))
    .expectNext("a")
    .expectNext("b")
    .verifyComplete();

See Testing for a full treatment.

docs.title: Other implementations
docs.text: Spring WebFlux is unopinionated about the reactive library. Any Publisher implementation can be a controller return type, and Spring adapts between supported reactive types automatically.

docs.title: RxJava 3
docs.text:
RxJava 3 implements Reactive Streams with Flowable (backpressured), Observable (unbackpressured), Single, Maybe, and Completable. RxJava 2 is end of life and removed from Spring's supported adapters; prefer RxJava 3 for new work.

// io.reactivex.rxjava3:rxjava
Flowable.just("a", "b", "c")
    .map(String::toUpperCase)
    .subscribe(System.out::println);

See RxJava 3 in a controller for the WebFlux integration.

docs.title: SmallRye Mutiny
docs.text:
SmallRye Mutiny is a Reactive Streams implementation from Red Hat, supported by Spring since Framework 5.3.10. Its two core types are Uni<T> (0..1, similar to Mono but accepts null) and Multi<T> (0..N, similar to Flux).

// io.smallrye.reactive:mutiny
Uni.createFrom().item("hello")
    .onItem().transform(String::toUpperCase)
    .subscribe().with(System.out::println);

See Mutiny in a controller for the WebFlux integration.

docs.title: The JDK Flow API
docs.text:
The JDK ships java.util.concurrent.Flow, which packages the Reactive Streams interfaces inside the JDK and adds a ready-made SubmissionPublisher implementation. The JDK also includes a reactive java.net.http.HttpClient built on the Flow API.

SubmissionPublisher<String> publisher = new SubmissionPublisher<>();
publisher.subscribe(new Flow.Subscriber<>() {
    @Override
    public void onSubscribe(Flow.Subscription subscription) {
        subscription.request(Long.MAX_VALUE);
    }

    @Override
    public void onNext(String item) {
        System.out.println("received: " + item);
    }

    @Override
    public void onError(Throwable throwable) {
    }

    @Override
    public void onComplete() {
        System.out.println("done");
    }
});

publisher.submit("hello");
publisher.close();

Spring adapts between Flow.Publisher and Reactive Streams types — see The JDK Flow API and the runnable java9 sample.

docs.title: Choosing an implementation
docs.text:
Library Core types Backpressure Notes Project Reactor Mono, Flux Yes Default in Spring; richest operator set; reactor-test for verification RxJava 3 Flowable, Observable, Single, Maybe, Completable Flowable only Adapted types supported in WebFlux controllers SmallRye Mutiny Uni, Multi Yes Simple, event-first API; Uni accepts null JDK Flow Flow.Publisher Yes JDK-native; minimal operators; useful for interop

For new Spring projects, start with Project Reactor: it is what Spring Data, Spring Security, Spring Session, and the WebFlux server internals are built on.

docs.title: How Spring WebFlux uses the reactive stack
docs.text:
Spring WebFlux builds on Reactive Streams and Project Reactor by default, but stays unopinionated about the reactive runtime. The key integration points:

  • Reactive return types. Controller methods and handler functions may return Mono<T>, Flux<T>, CompletableFuture<T>, or any org.reactivestreams.Publisher<T>. Spring adapts between supported reactive types automatically.
  • Two programming models. Annotated controllers (@RestController with @GetMapping, @PostMapping, and friends) or functional handlers (RouterFunction + HandlerFunction) — see the Reactive Web chapter.
  • A reactive HTTP client. WebClient performs non-blocking HTTP requests and integrates with Reactor and other reactive types — see WebClient.
  • Server runtimes. Reactor Netty is the default server for Spring Boot's WebFlux starter; Tomcat, Jetty, and Undertow are also supported — see the bootstrapping options in Create a WebFlux application from scratch.
  • The wider ecosystem. Spring Data (R2DBC, reactive repositories), Spring Security (ServerHttpSecurity, reactive user details), and Spring Session (reactive WebSession storage) all accept and return Reactive Streams types — the following chapters cover each of them.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: Testing reactive code needs tools that understand asynchrony: assertions on sequences of signals rather than single values, mocks for suspending or publisher-returning methods, and integration tests that never block. The Spring reactive stack ships a layered toolkit, and every sample in this repository exercises at least one layer.

docs.text:

  2. Data Operations with Testcontainers — real databases in Docker for the data layer: the plain Spring initializer pattern and the Boot @DynamicPropertySource/@ServiceConnection styles.
  3. Spring Test Context and Slices — SpringJUnitConfig, @SpringBootTest, and the Boot test slices (@WebFluxTest, @JsonTest, @DataMongoTest, and friends).
