docs.title: StepVerifier: verify a Publisher
docs.text:
StepVerifier (from the reactor-test module) is the foundation: it subscribes to a Publisher and asserts the exact sequence of signals — onNext values, then completion or error:

StepVerifier.create(posts.findAll())
    .consumeNextWith(p -> assertEquals("post one", p.getTitle()))
    .consumeNextWith(p -> assertEquals("post two", p.getTitle()))
    .expectComplete()
    .verify();

Common patterns used across the samples:

// assert a count of elements
postClient.allPosts()
        .as(StepVerifier::create)
        .expectNextCount(2)
        .verifyComplete();

// assert with custom assertions and cancellation
counter.getInvocationCount()
        .as(StepVerifier::create)
        .consumeNextWith(count -> assertThat(count).isGreaterThan(0))
        .thenCancel()
        .verify();

// build into the call chain with as(StepVerifier::create)
posts.findByTitleLike("one")
    .as(StepVerifier::create)
    .consumeNextWith(p -> assertEquals("Post one", p.getTitle()))
    .verifyComplete();

The key methods:

  • expectNext(T... values) / expectNextCount(long) — assert the emitted values or their count
  • consumeNextWith(Consumer) — assert each element with a custom assertion
  • expectError(Class) / verifyComplete() — terminate the verification
  • thenCancel() — cancel the subscription mid-stream
  • as(StepVerifier::create) — adapt an existing Mono/Flux chain into a verifier

StepVerifier appears everywhere in this book — from repository tests in the Data Operations chapter to the WebClient tests in Web Programming. The next page moves up the stack to testing the web layer itself.

docs.title: Testing in Kotlin
docs.text:
Kotlin tests keep the same layered structure as the Java ones — StepVerifier, WebTestClient, Testcontainers — with a Kotlin-native toolkit on top: Kotest assertion matchers, MockK for suspending functions, Spring MockK for bean overrides, and kotlinx-coroutines-test for coroutine lifecycles.

The samples referenced here are kotlin-co and boot-kotlin-co in this repository, plus boot-kotlin-co in the spring6-sandbox repository.

docs.title: Test dependencies
docs.text:
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.jetbrains.kotlinx</groupId>
    <artifactId>kotlinx-coroutines-test</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.kotest</groupId>
    <artifactId>kotest-assertions-core-jvm</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.mockk</groupId>
    <artifactId>mockk-jvm</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.ninja-squad</groupId>
    <artifactId>springmockk</artifactId>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>

docs.title: MockK: mocking suspending functions
docs.text:
MockK mirrors the Mockito vocabulary for coroutines: coEvery stubs a suspend call, coVerify asserts it, and coEvery { ... } throws ... drives the error paths:

coEvery { postRepository.findByTitleContains(any()) } returns
        flowOf(Post(id = 1, title = "test title", content = "test content"))

coEvery { postRepository.findById(any()) } throws PostNotFoundException(id)

coVerify(exactly = 0) { postRepository.findByTitleContains(any()) }

Flow-returning methods are stubbed with flowOf(...), and clearAllMocks() resets between tests.

docs.title: Spring MockK: @MockkBean and @MockkSpyBean
docs.text:
Spring MockK is the Kotlines counterpart of @MockitoBean/@MockitoSpyBean (see Testing Web Components):

  • @MockkBean — replace a bean with a MockK mock; stub it with coEvery { ... } returns ...
  • @MockkSpyBean — wrap the real bean in a spy: real behavior by default, coEvery overrides selected calls

The boot-kotlin-co sample uses @MockkBean inside a @WebFluxTest slice:

@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
@WebFluxTest(controllers = [PostController::class])
class PostControllerTest {

    @MockkBean
    private lateinit var postRepository: PostRepository

    @Autowired
    private lateinit var client: WebTestClient

    @Test
    fun `get posts by title with invalid title`() = runTest {
        coEvery { postRepository.findByTitleContains(any()) } returns
                flowOf(Post(id = 1, title = "test title", content = "test content"))

        client.get().uri("/byTitle?title=")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isBadRequest

        coVerify(exactly = 0) { postRepository.findByTitleContains(any()) }
    }

    @Test
    fun `get post that not found`() = runTest {
        val id = 1L
        coEvery { postRepository.findById(any()) } throws PostNotFoundException(id)

        client.get().uri("/$id")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isNotFound

        coVerify(exactly = 1) { postRepository.findById(any()) }
    }
}

docs.title: kotlinx-coroutines-test: runTest
docs.text:
Every test that touches coroutine code runs under runTest { } — it skips real delays and completes when the coroutine tree settles, even for the WebTestClient exchange calls above. The repository tests use the same shape:

@Test
fun `test save and query`() = runTest {
    val saved = template.insert(Post(title = "test", content = "content of test")).awaitSingle()
    saved.id shouldNotBe null

    val postById = posts.findById(saved.id!!)
    postById shouldNotBe null
    postById!!.title shouldBe "test"
}

The awaitSingle() extension (from kotlinx.coroutines.reactor) bridges the reactive Mono into the coroutine; awaitSingleOrNull(), awaitFirst(), and awaitToList() cover the other shapes — see the transaction extensions in Coroutines.

docs.title: Kotest assertions
docs.text:
Kotest contributes the infix assertion matchers used across the Kotlin samples — shouldBe, shouldNotBe, shouldContain, and friends:

import io.kotest.matchers.shouldBe
import io.kotest.matchers.shouldNotBe

posts shouldNotBe null
postById!!.title shouldBe "test"

Kotest matchers compose with everything above — inside runTest, inside StepVerifier.consumeNextWith, or alongside AssertJ in mixed codebases. They work on plain JUnit 5 tests (as the samples do) or inside Kotest's own spec styles if you prefer a full Kotest test framework.

docs.title: A complete plain Spring test
docs.text:
The kotlin-co sample assembles the pieces — SpringJUnitConfig, a manually registered MockK bean, bindToController, and Kotest matchers — without Boot:

@SpringJUnitConfig(classes = [TestConfig::class])
class PostControllerTest {

    @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
    @ComponentScan(basePackageClasses = [PostController::class])
    internal class TestConfig {

        @Bean
        @Primary
        fun mockPostRepository(): PostRepository = mockk<PostRepository>()
    }

    @Autowired
    lateinit var posts: PostRepository

    lateinit var client: WebTestClient

    @BeforeEach
    fun setup() {
        client = WebTestClient.bindToController(PostController(posts))
            .configureClient()
            .build()
    }

    @AfterEach
    fun teardown() {
        clearAllMocks()
    }

    @Test
    fun `get post by id`() = runTest {
        val id = UUID.randomUUID().toString()
        coEvery { posts.findById(any()) } returns
                Post(id = id, title = "test title", content = "content of test title")

        client.get().uri("/posts/$id")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isOk
            .expectBody().jsonPath("$.title").isEqualTo("test title")
    }
}

When Boot's bean-override machinery is available, prefer @MockkBean over the manual @Primary mock bean — the manual registration shown here is what makes the same test work in plain Spring modules.

docs.title: Spring Test Context and Slices
docs.text: Spring Test provides a spectrum of test contexts, from a targeted slice to the full application. This page maps the spectrum as the samples use it: SpringJUnitConfig for plain Spring modules, @SpringBootTest for full Boot contexts, and the Boot test slices that load only what a layer needs.

docs.title: SpringJUnitConfig: plain Spring without Boot
docs.text:
Non-Boot samples test with SpringJUnitConfig — the JUnit 5 extension that builds an ApplicationContext from the given configuration classes without any Boot machinery:

@SpringJUnitConfig(classes = Application.class)
@ActiveProfiles("test")   // disables the Netty @Profile("default") server bean
public class ApplicationTests {

    @Autowired
    ApplicationContext context;

    WebTestClient rest;

    @BeforeEach
    public void setup() {
        this.rest = WebTestClient
                .bindToApplicationContext(this.context)
                .configureClient()
                .build();
    }

    @Test
    public void getAllPostsWillBeOk() {
        this.rest
                .get()
                .uri("/posts")
                .exchange()
                .expectStatus().isOk();
    }
}

This pattern runs across the plain Spring samples — the integration sample's ApplicationTests and PostControllerTest show it with bindToApplicationContext and the narrower bindToController:

this.rest = WebTestClient.bindToController(this.ctrl)
        .configureClient()
        .build();

docs.title: SpringBootTest: the full context
docs.text:
@SpringBootTest boots the complete application. With WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT it starts the real server on a free port, and @AutoConfigureWebTestClient injects a client ready to talk to it:

@AutoConfigureWebTestClient
@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
public class IntegrationTests {

    @Autowired
    WebTestClient client;

    @Test
    public void getAllPosts() {
        client.get().uri("/posts")
                .exchange()
                .expectStatus().isOk()
                .expectBody().jsonPath("$.size()").isEqualTo(2);
    }
}

Combine it with the Testcontainers styles from Data Operations with Testcontainers (@ServiceConnection or @DynamicPropertySource) and the full stack — web layer, data layer, real database — runs in one test.

docs.title: Integration tests over a real server
docs.text:
Some contracts only exist over the wire. The integration sample binds its own Reactor Netty server bean and a server-bound WebTestClient:

@SpringJUnitConfig(classes = Application.class)
public class IntegrationTests {

    @Autowired
    HttpServer httpServer;

    private DisposableServer disposableServer;

    @BeforeEach
    public void setup() {
        this.disposableServer = this.httpServer.bindNow();
        this.client = WebTestClient
                .bindToServer()
                .responseTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(5000))
                .baseUrl("http://localhost:" + this.port)
                .build();
    }

    @AfterEach
    public void tearDown() {
        this.disposableServer.disposeNow();
    }

    @Test
    public void getAllPostsWillBeOk_viaIntegration() {
        this.client
                .get()
                .uri("/all")
                .exchange()
                .expectStatus().isOk();
    }
}

This is the shape to use for SSE streams, WebSocket handshakes, and cookie/header contracts — see session-header for a worked example.

docs.title: Test slices
docs.text:
Boot's test slices load only the auto-configuration a layer needs, keeping tests fast and focused:

Slice Loads Typical use @WebFluxTest WebFlux infrastructure for the given controllers Controller and filter tests with mocked dependencies — see Testing Web Components @JsonTest JSON serializers/deserializers only (Jackson, and @JsonTester injection) Round-trip serialization assertions without any web layer @DataMongoTest Spring Data Mongo repositories and ReactiveMongoTemplate Repository tests against a real Mongo — pair with Testcontainers @DataR2dbcTest Spring Data R2DBC repositories, DatabaseClient R2DBC repository tests @DataNeo4jTest Spring Data Neo4j repositories Neo4j repository tests — see Neo4j — Testing

A @DataMongoTest repository test from the boot-data-mongo sample — the slice plus a @ServiceConnection container gives a complete database test with no web layer loaded:

@DataMongoTest
@Import(TestcontainersConfiguration.class)
@ActiveProfiles("test")
public class PostRepositoryTest {

    @Autowired
    ReactiveMongoTemplate reactiveMongoTemplate;

    @Autowired
    PostRepository postRepository;
}

Slices and transactions

Reactive slices are not transactional by default. When a slice (for example @DataNeo4jTest) applies test-managed transactions that the reactive stack cannot drive, add @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.NEVER) — the Neo4j — Testing page walks through the details.

A @JsonTest follows the same recipe — the slice auto-configures the JSON beans and injects a tester:

@JsonTest
class PostJsonTest {

    @Autowired
    JacksonTester<Post> json;

    @Test
    void serialize() throws Exception {
        var post = new Post(UUID.randomUUID(), "test title", "content");
        assertThat(json.write(post)).extractingJsonPathStringValue("$.title").isEqualTo("test title");
    }
}

The slices pair naturally with the bean-override annotations: @WebFluxTest + @MockitoBean for the web layer, data slices + Testcontainers for the persistence layer.

docs.title: Data Operations with Testcontainers
docs.text:
Repository tests need a real database. Testcontainers starts the store in a Docker container for the duration of the test and tears it down afterwards. The samples use two wiring styles — one for plain Spring applications and one for Spring Boot — plus Boot's automatic @ServiceConnection variant.

Tip

Pair Testcontainers with StepVerifier (see Testing) to assert the reactive query results.

docs.title: Plain Spring: ApplicationContextInitializer
docs.text:
The non-Boot samples (cache, the r2dbc-* modules) implement an ApplicationContextInitializer that starts the container, maps its properties into the environment, and stops it when the context closes:

@TestConfiguration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
public class ContainersConfiguration implements ApplicationContextInitializer<ConfigurableApplicationContext> {

    private static final PostgreSQLContainer POSTGRES = new PostgreSQLContainer(
            DockerImageName.parse("postgres:18.4-alpine"))
            .withCopyFileToContainer(
                    MountableFile.forClasspathResource("init.sql"),
                    "/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/init.sql");

    @Override
    public void initialize(ConfigurableApplicationContext context) {
        if (!POSTGRES.isRunning()) {
            POSTGRES.start();
        }
        context.addApplicationListener((ContextClosedEvent event) -> POSTGRES.stop());
        TestPropertyValues.of(
                "r2dbc.host=" + POSTGRES.getHost(),
                "r2dbc.port=" + POSTGRES.getFirstMappedPort(),
                "r2dbc.username=" + POSTGRES.getUsername(),
                "r2dbc.password=" + POSTGRES.getPassword(),
                "r2dbc.database=" + POSTGRES.getDatabaseName()
        ).applyTo(context.getEnvironment());
    }
}

The initializer is applied through @ContextConfiguration, so it is reusable across test classes:

@ContextConfiguration(initializers = { ContainersConfiguration.class })
@SpringJUnitConfig(classes = { PostRepositoryTest.TestConfig.class })
public class PostRepositoryTest {

    @Autowired
    PostRepository posts;

    @Test
    public void testSaveAll() {
        var post = posts.save(Post.of("test", "content")).block();
        assertThat(posts.findById(post.id()).block()).isNotNull();
    }
}

Because the properties use the application's own keys (r2dbc.* in the samples), no container library knowledge leaks into the configuration classes — see the cache sample for the complete pattern, and the r2dbc-connection-factories tests for raw-driver variants.

docs.title: Spring Boot with @DynamicPropertySource
docs.text:
For Boot applications, the @Testcontainers + @Container + @DynamicPropertySource combination starts the container with the JUnit lifecycle and maps its runtime values into arbitrary property keys. From the boot-data-mongo-template sample:

@DataMongoTest
@Import({PostRepository.class, TestcontainersConfiguration.class})
public class PostRepositoryTest {

    @Container
    static MongoDBContainer mongoDBContainer = new MongoDBContainer(DockerImageName.parse("mongo:latest"));

    @DynamicPropertySource
    static void mongoProperties(DynamicPropertyRegistry registry) {
        registry.add("spring.data.mongodb.uri", mongoDBContainer::getReplicaSetUrl);
    }

    @Autowired
    ReactiveMongoTemplate reactiveMongoTemplate;

    @Autowired
    PostRepository postRepository;
}

Notes:

  • @Testcontainers (class level) enables the JUnit extension; a static @Container field starts before all tests and stops after them.
  • The @DynamicPropertySource method receives a DynamicPropertyRegistry — register the connection properties as suppliers, resolved lazily once the container is up.
  • Any property key works here: spring.data.mongodb.uri, spring.r2dbc.url, spring.neo4j.uri, or custom keys.

docs.title: Spring Boot with @ServiceConnection
docs.text:
Boot 3.1+ removes even the property mapping: a container bean annotated with @ServiceConnection contributes the connection properties automatically — Boot recognizes the container type and registers the right properties. From the boot-data-mongo sample:

@TestConfiguration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class TestcontainersConfiguration {

    @Bean
    @ServiceConnection
    MongoDBContainer mongoDbContainer() {
        return new MongoDBContainer(DockerImageName.parse("mongo:latest"));
    }
}

@DataMongoTest
@Import(TestcontainersConfiguration.class)
@ActiveProfiles("test")
public class PostRepositoryTest {

    @Autowired
    ReactiveMongoTemplate reactiveMongoTemplate;

    @Autowired
    PostRepository postRepository;
}

No @DynamicPropertySource, no property names — Boot wires spring.data.mongodb.uri (or spring.r2dbc.url for a PostgreSQLContainer, spring.neo4j.uri for a Neo4jContainer, and so on) from the container itself. The same pattern appears with CassandraContainer, CouchbaseContainer, ElasticsearchContainer, and Neo4jContainer across the Boot data samples — see the Data Operations chapter pages for each store's snippet.

docs.title: Choosing a style
docs.text: Style Use when ApplicationContextInitializer + TestPropertyValues Plain Spring (no Boot) tests; reusable initializer shared by many test classes @Testcontainers + @DynamicPropertySource Boot tests needing explicit control of property keys or container options @ServiceConnection Boot tests with a supported container type — the least code, zero property names

docs.title: Testing Web Components
docs.text:
The web layer is tested with WebTestClient, which mirrors the WebClient API and adds response assertions. This page covers testing annotated controllers, exception handling, RouterFunctions, and filters — with the dependencies mocked or spied through Spring's bean overriding annotations.

The tests run on JUnit 5 with Mockito for stubbing; for the Kotlin equivalents see Testing in Kotlin.

docs.title: A controller test with a mocked dependency
docs.text:
@WebFluxTest(controllers = ...) loads only the web configuration for the given controller — no database, no full context. The controller's dependencies are replaced with @MockitoBean (from org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.mockito), and Mockito stubs their publisher-returning methods:

@WebFluxTest(controllers = PostController.class)
public class PostControllerTest {

    @Autowired
    WebTestClient client;

    @MockitoBean
    PostRepository posts;

    @Test
    public void getAllPosts() {
        when(this.posts.findAll()).thenReturn(Flux.just(
                Post.builder().id(UUID.randomUUID()).title("post one").content("content of post one").build(),
                Post.builder().id(UUID.randomUUID()).title("post two").content("content of post two").build()
        ));
        client.get().uri("/posts")
                .exchange()
                .expectStatus().isOk()
                .expectBody().jsonPath("$.size()").isEqualTo(2);

        verify(this.posts, times(1)).findAll();
        verifyNoMoreInteractions(this.posts);
    }
}

Notes:

  • @WebFluxTest auto-configures a WebTestClient bound to the mock web environment — inject it with @Autowired.
  • @MockitoBean replaces the bean in the context with a Mockito mock; when(...)/given(...) stub the reactive methods to return Flux.just(...) or Mono.just(...).
  • The BDD style works too: given(this.posts.findAll()).willReturn(Flux.just(post1, post2)).

Boot 3 vs Boot 4

Spring Boot 3 used @MockBean (deprecated and removed in Boot 4); Spring Framework 6.2+ / Boot 4 use @MockitoBean and @MockitoSpyBean from org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.mockito.

docs.title: Mocks and spies
docs.text:
• @MockitoBean — replace a bean entirely with a mock. Unstubbed publisher-returning methods return empty publishers.
  • @MockitoSpyBean — wrap the real bean in a spy: real methods run unless explicitly stubbed, and interactions are still verifiable. Use it when the collaborator's real behavior matters and you only need to observe or tweak a few calls:
@MockitoSpyBean
PostRepository posts;

Both annotations live in the same package as @MockitoBean and work in any Spring test — slices, @SpringBootTest, or plain SpringJUnitConfig tests.

docs.title: Exception handling and status codes
docs.text:
Exception handlers are exercised by driving the client into the error path and asserting the mapped status — here a not-found domain exception maps to 404 through the controller's @ExceptionHandler:

@Test
fun `get post that not found`() = runTest {
    val id = 1L
    coEvery { postRepository.findById(any()) } throws PostNotFoundException(id)

    client.get().uri("/$id")
        .exchange()
        .expectStatus().isNotFound

    coVerify(exactly = 1) { postRepository.findById(any()) }
}

The Java pattern is identical with Mockito: stub the dependency to return Mono.error(new PostNotFoundException(id)), then expectStatus().isNotFound(). Assert the body of RFC 9457 ProblemDetail responses with expectBody(ProblemDetail.class) when a handler returns one.

docs.title: Testing RouterFunctions
docs.text:
Functional routes are tested by binding the client to the RouterFunction bean. From the boot-start-routes sample:

@AutoConfigureWebTestClient
@SpringBootTest
// create a `WebTestClient` with essential options from application context automatically,
// it works on both mock env or a real server.
public class ApplicationTest {

    @Autowired
    RouterFunction<ServerResponse> routerFunction;

    @MockitoBean
    PostRepository posts;

    WebTestClient client;

    @BeforeEach
    void setUp() {
        this.client = WebTestClient.bindToRouterFunction(this.routerFunction)
                .configureClient()
                .build();
    }

    @Test
    public void getAllPosts() {
        // stub the repository, call client.get().uri("/posts")...
    }
}

bindToRouterFunction handles a single RouterFunction; bindToApplicationContext(context) loads the full handler infrastructure (filters, exception handlers) without a socket, and bindToWebHandler(...) sits between the two.

docs.title: Testing filters
docs.text:
Filters are verified by importing them into a @WebFluxTest slice and asserting the outcome with and without the triggering condition — the spring6-sandbox filter tests do exactly that for a security-check filter:

@WebFluxTest(controllers = HelloController.class)
class WebFilterTests {

    @TestConfiguration
    @Import(value = SecurityWebFilter.class)
    class TestConfig

    @Autowired
    WebTestClient client;

    @Test
    void `authentication failed with no user params`() = runTest {
        client.get().uri("/hello")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isUnauthorized
    }

    @Test
    void `authentication passed with user params`() = runTest {
        client.get().uri("/hello?user=Hantsy")
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isOk
    }
}

A Java WebFilter test follows the same shape: @Import the filter, request a route the filter protects, assert 401 without the precondition and 200 with it.

docs.title: Against a running server
docs.text: Slice tests exercise the request-handling stack only. When a test needs the real HTTP contract — SSE, WebSocket, cookies — bind the client to a live server instead; see Spring Test Context and Slices.

docs.title: API Versioning
docs.text:
Spring Framework 7 adds built-in API versioning support on both the server and the client side. The version can be carried in a URI path segment, a request parameter, an HTTP header, or a media type parameter, and routes can be mapped per version with a version attribute on the mapping annotations.

This page covers the reactive (WebFlux) flavor; the same concepts apply to the Servlet stack. The samples referenced here are api-versioning-webflux and boot-api-versioning-webflux in the spring7-sandbox repository — see its API Versioning guide for the full treatment including WebMVC.

docs.title: Server-side configuration
docs.text:
Implement WebFluxConfigurer and override configureApiVersioning to declare where the version is read from and which versions are supported:

@Configuration
@EnableWebFlux
public class WebConfig implements WebFluxConfigurer {

    @Override
    public void configureApiVersioning(ApiVersionConfigurer configurer) {
        configurer
                //.usePathSegment(0)
                .useRequestHeader("X-API-Version")
                //.useRequestParam("version")

                .setDefaultVersion("1.0")
                // When a defaultVersion is also set, this is automatically set to false.
                // .setVersionRequired(true)

                // default is SemanticApiVersionParser
                //.setVersionParser(new SemanticApiVersionParser())

                // set detectSupportedVersions(false) when adding supported versions
                .detectSupportedVersions(false)
                .addSupportedVersions("1.0", "1.1", "2.0");
    }
}

The version resolution strategies, exactly one of which is active at a time:

  • usePathSegment(0) — read the version from a URI path segment, for example /api/v1/resource
  • useRequestHeader("X-API-Version") — read it from an HTTP header, for example X-API-Version: 1
  • useRequestParam("version") — read it from a request parameter, for example /api/resource?version=1
  • useMediaTypeParameter(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON, "version") — append a version parameter to the Accept header value, for example application/json;version=1

Versions are parsed with SemanticApiVersionParser by default, and setDefaultVersion("1.0") handles requests that carry no version at all.

docs.title: Versioned routes
docs.text:
Mapping annotations accept a version attribute. Requests without a version map to the unversioned method; requests carrying a version map to the method that declares it:

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/hello")
public class GreetingController {

    @GetMapping()
    public String helloDefault() {
        return "Hello v1.0(Default)";
    }

    @GetMapping(version = "1.1")
    public String helloV1_1() {
        return "Hello v1.1";
    }

    @GetMapping(version = "2.0")
    public String helloV2_0() {
        return "Hello v2.0";
    }
}

In a Spring Boot 4 WebFlux application, the same WebConfig applies, and Boot exposes properties for it — the WebMVC counterpart reads spring.mvc.api-versioning.* (see the spring7-sandbox guide for the full property list).

docs.title: Client-side versioning with WebClient
docs.text:
WebClient participates in versioning through ApiVersionInserter — it declares where the version is written — and defaultApiVersion sets a fallback for requests that do not name one:

this.client = WebClient.builder()
        .baseUrl("http://localhost:" + this.port)
        .defaultApiVersion("1.0")
        .apiVersionInserter(ApiVersionInserter.builder()
                .useHeader("X-API-Version")
                //.usePathSegment(0)
                //.useQueryParam("version")
                //.withVersionFormatter(ApiVersionFormatter)
                .build()
        )
        .build();

The inserter strategies mirror the server side — useHeader, usePathSegment, useQueryParam, or withVersionFormatter for custom rendering — and must agree with how the server resolves versions.

Per-request versions override the default:

this.client.get().uri("/hello")
        .apiVersion("1.1")
        .retrieve()
        .bodyToMono(String.class)

A full integration test drives all three versions against the running server:

@SpringJUnitConfig(classes = Application.class)
public class IntegrationTests {

    @Autowired
    HttpServer httpServer;

    @BeforeEach
    public void setup() {
        this.disposableServer = this.httpServer.bindNow(Duration.ofMillis(5_000));
        this.client = WebClient.builder()
                .baseUrl("http://localhost:" + this.port)
                .defaultApiVersion("1.0")
                .apiVersionInserter(ApiVersionInserter.builder()
                        .useHeader("X-API-Version")
                        .build())
                .build();
    }

    @Test
    public void testHello1_1() {
        this.client.get().uri("/hello")
                .apiVersion("1.1")
                .retrieve()
                .bodyToMono(String.class)
                .as(StepVerifier::create)
                .expectNext("Hello v1.1")
                .verifyComplete();
    }
}

docs.title: Testing with WebTestClient
docs.text:
WebTestClient supports the same contract. In a @WebFluxTest slice, register a WebTestClientBuilderCustomizer (in Boot 4 it lives in the org.springframework.boot.webtestclient.autoconfigure package) to configure the versioning on the test client:

@WebFluxTest(controllers = GreetingController.class)
public class GreetingControllerTest {

    @TestConfiguration
    static class TestConfig {

        @Bean
        WebTestClientBuilderCustomizer testClientBuilderCustomizer() {
            return builder -> builder.defaultApiVersion("1.0")
                    .apiVersionInserter(ApiVersionInserter.useHeader("X-API-Version"))
                    .build();
        }
    }

    @Autowired
    WebTestClient webTestClient;

    @Test
    void testHello1_1() {
        this.webTestClient.get().uri("/hello")
                .apiVersion("1.1")
                .exchange()
                .expectBody(String.class).isEqualTo("Hello v1.1");
    }
}

docs.title: WebClient and Reactive HTTP Clients
docs.text:
In the Servlet stack, RestTemplate and AsyncRestTemplate perform HTTP requests. In the WebFlux stack, Spring adds WebClient — a non-blocking, reactive HTTP client that integrates with Reactor and other reactive types.

WebClient supports streaming request and response bodies, runs on several pluggable HTTP client libraries, and is the foundation for consuming other reactive services.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
The simplest way to create a client is a static factory. The following example sends a GET request to the /posts URI and retrieves posts:

WebClient client = WebClient.create("http://localhost:8080");
client
    .get()
    .uri("/posts")
    .retrieve()
    .bodyToFlux(Post.class)
    .log()
    .subscribe(post -> System.out.println("post: " + post));

docs.title: Building a client
docs.text:
For more control, use the builder. It lets you configure the ClientHttpConnector (the underlying HTTP client), the codecs, ExchangeStrategies, default headers, and filters:

var reactorHttpClient = HttpClient.create()
        .wiretap("reactor.netty.http.client.HttpClient", LogLevel.DEBUG,
                AdvancedByteBufFormat.TEXTUAL)
        .option(ChannelOption.CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MILLIS, 5000);

WebClient client = WebClient.builder()
    .clientConnector(new ReactorClientHttpConnector(reactorHttpClient))
    .codecs(
        clientCodecConfigurer -> {
            // use defaultCodecs() to apply the default codecs
            // clientCodecConfigurer.defaultCodecs();

            // alter a registered encoder/decoder based on the default config.
            // clientCodecConfigurer.defaultCodecs().jacksonJsonEncoder(...)

            // or use customCodecs to register codecs from scratch.
            clientCodecConfigurer.customCodecs()
                    .register(new JacksonJsonDecoder(objectMapper));
            clientCodecConfigurer.customCodecs()
                    .register(new JacksonJsonEncoder(objectMapper));
        }
    )
    .exchangeStrategies(ExchangeStrategies.withDefaults())
    .baseUrl("http://localhost:8080")
    .build();

docs.title: A typed client class
docs.text:
Rather than scattering WebClient calls through the application, wrap them in a dedicated client class. The sample uses exchangeToMono/exchangeToFlux to inspect the response status and convert error responses with response.createError():

@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class PostClient {

    private final WebClient client;

    Flux<Post> allPosts() {
        return client.get()
                .uri("/posts")
                .accept(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .exchangeToFlux(response -> response.bodyToFlux(Post.class));
    }

    Mono<Post> getById(UUID id) {
        return client.get()
                .uri(uriBuilder -> uriBuilder.path("/posts/{id}").build(id))
                .accept(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .exchangeToMono(response -> {
                    if (response.statusCode().equals(HttpStatus.OK)) {
                        return response.bodyToMono(Post.class);
                    }
                    return response.createError();
                });
    }

    Mono<ResponseEntity<Void>> save(Post post) {
        return client.post()
                .uri("/posts")
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .bodyValue(post)
                .exchangeToMono(response -> {
                    if (response.statusCode().equals(HttpStatus.CREATED)) {
                        return response.toBodilessEntity();
                    }
                    return response.createError();
                });
    }

    Mono<ResponseEntity<Void>> update(UUID id, Post post) {
        return client.put()
                .uri(uriBuilder -> uriBuilder.path("/posts/{id}").build(id))
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .bodyValue(post)
                .exchangeToMono(response -> {
                    if (response.statusCode().equals(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT)) {
                        return response.toBodilessEntity();
                    }
                    return response.createError();
                });
    }

    Mono<ResponseEntity<Void>> delete(UUID id) {
        return client.delete()
                .uri(uriBuilder -> uriBuilder.path("/posts/{id}").build(id))
                .exchangeToMono(response -> {
                    if (response.statusCode().equals(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT)) {
                        return response.toBodilessEntity();
                    }
                    return response.createError();
                });
    }
}

Then drive the flows in an application class:

public static void main(String[] args) {
    var applicationContext = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(Application.class);
    var postClient = applicationContext.getBean(PostClient.class);

    postClient.allPosts().subscribe(data -> log.debug("post: {}", data));

    postClient.save(new Post(null, "test", "test content", Status.DRAFT, null))
            .log()
            .flatMap(saved -> {
                var uri = saved.getHeaders().getLocation().toString();
                var strings = uri.split("/");
                return client.getById(UUID.fromString(strings[strings.length - 1]));
            })
            .flatMap(post -> client.update(post.id(),
                    new Post(null, "updated test", "updated content", Status.PENDING_MODERATION, null)))
            .subscribe(responseEntity -> log.debug("updated status: {}", responseEntity));
}

For the complete codes, check spring-reactive-sample/client.

docs.title: Choosing the HTTP client connector
docs.text:
The ClientHttpConnector abstracts the underlying HTTP client. By default, WebClient uses ReactorClientHttpConnector (Reactor Netty). Spring also ships connectors for other clients:

Connector Underlying client Extra dependency ReactorClientHttpConnector (default) Reactor Netty none (in WebFlux) JettyClientHttpConnector Jetty Reactive HttpClient org.eclipse.jetty:jetty-reactive-httpclient JdkClientHttpConnector JDK java.net.http.HttpClient none HttpComponentsClientHttpConnector Apache HttpClient 5 org.apache.httpcomponents.client5:httpclient5

docs.title: Reactor Netty (default)
docs.text:
var reactorHttpClient = HttpClient.create()
        .wiretap("reactor.netty.http.client.HttpClient", LogLevel.DEBUG,
                AdvancedByteBufFormat.TEXTUAL)
        .option(ChannelOption.CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MILLIS, 5000);

var connector = new ReactorClientHttpConnector(reactorHttpClient);

docs.title: Jetty Reactive HttpClient
docs.text:
var jettyHttpClient = new org.eclipse.jetty.client.HttpClient();
jettyHttpClient.setConnectTimeout(5000L);
jettyHttpClient.start();
var connector = new JettyClientHttpConnector(jettyHttpClient);

Add the dependency:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.eclipse.jetty</groupId>
    <artifactId>jetty-reactive-httpclient</artifactId>
</dependency>

docs.title: JDK HttpClient
docs.text:
The built-in JDK java.net.http.HttpClient needs no extra dependency:

var jvmHttpClient = java.net.http.HttpClient.newBuilder()
        .executor(Executors.newCachedThreadPool())
        .version(java.net.http.HttpClient.Version.HTTP_2)
        .build();
var connector = new JdkClientHttpConnector(jvmHttpClient);

docs.title: Apache HttpClient 5
docs.text:
var httpAsyncClient = org.apache.hc.client5.http.impl.async.HttpAsyncClients.createHttp2Default();
var connector = new HttpComponentsClientHttpConnector(httpAsyncClient);

Add the dependency:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.apache.httpcomponents.client5</groupId>
    <artifactId>httpclient5</artifactId>
</dependency>

Each connector swaps in with one builder call — .clientConnector(connector) — while the PostClient layer above stays untouched. For the complete codes of each variant, check client-jetty, client-jdk11-httpclient, and client-apache-httpclient5.

docs.title: Mocking a target Http API with WireMock
docs.text:
The samples test PostClient against WireMock using @WireMockTest(httpPort = 8080) — the same port the client targets — and assert the reactive sequences with StepVerifier:

@SpringJUnitConfig(classes = { ClientConfig.class, Jackson2ObjectMapperConfig.class })
@WireMockTest(httpPort = 8080)
public class PostClientTest {

    @Autowired
    PostClient postClient;

    @SneakyThrows
    @Test
    public void testGetAllPosts() {
        var data = List.of(
                new Post(UUID.randomUUID(), "title1", "content1", Status.DRAFT, LocalDateTime.now()),
                new Post(UUID.randomUUID(), "title2", "content2", Status.PUBLISHED, LocalDateTime.now())
        );
        stubFor(get("/posts")
                .willReturn(aResponse()
                        .withHeader("Content-Type", "application/json")
                        .withResponseBody(Body.fromJsonBytes(Json.toByteArray(data)))));

        postClient.allPosts()
                .as(StepVerifier::create)
                .expectNextCount(2)
                .verifyComplete();

        verify(getRequestedFor(urlEqualTo("/posts"))
                .withHeader("Accept", equalTo("application/json")));
    }

    @SneakyThrows
    @Test
    public void testCreatePost() {
        var id = UUID.randomUUID();
        var data = new Post(null, "title1", "content1", Status.DRAFT, null);

        stubFor(post("/posts")
                .willReturn(aResponse()
                        .withHeader("Location", "/posts/" + id)
                        .withStatus(201)));

        postClient.save(data)
                .as(StepVerifier::create)
                .consumeNextWith(entity -> {
                    assertThat(entity.getHeaders().getLocation().toString()).isEqualTo("/posts/" + id);
                    assertThat(entity.getStatusCode().value()).isEqualTo(201);
                })
                .verifyComplete();
    }
}

See Testing for the full picture of reactive testing utilities.

docs.title: WebTestClient
docs.text:
Another client utility class is WebTestClient, which is used for testing the server side.

@WebFluxTest(controllers = MessageController.class)
public class DemoApplicationTests {

    @Autowired
    WebTestClient client;

    @Test
    public void getAllMessagesShouldBeOk() {
        client.get().uri("/").exchange().expectStatus().isOk();
    }
}

The usage of the WebTestClient API is very similar to WebClient, but it provides methods to assert the response result.

Note

Although WebClient and WebTestClient look similar, WebTestClient is a distinct test utility and is not derived from WebClient.

docs.title: Handling Web Exceptions
docs.text:
When exposing RESTful APIs you can choose between @RestController and functional RouterFunction routes.

The former is simple. If you have some experience with Spring WebMvc, it is easy to update your knowledge. Just need to use newer Reactor specific Mono and Flux instead in your codes.

The exception handling in reactive @RestController is similar to the one in WebMVC.

  1. Create an Exception class.

    public class PostNotFoundException extends RuntimeException {
    public PostNotFoundException(Long id) {
        super("Post:" + id +" is not found.");
    }
}

  2. Throw exception in your codes.

    @GetMapping(value = "/{id}")
public Mono<Post> get(@PathVariable(value = "id") Long id) {
    return this.posts.findById(id).switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(new PostNotFoundException(id)));
}

  3. Create a standalone @ControllerAdvice annotated class or @ExceptionHandler annotated method in your controller class to handle the exceptions.

    @RestControllerAdvice
@Slf4j
class RestExceptionHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(PostNotFoundException.class)
    public ResponseEntity<?> postNotFound(PostNotFoundException ex) {
        log.debug("handling exception: {}", ex.toString());
        return ResponseEntity.notFound().build();
    }

}

@RestControllerAdvice only works for @RestController.

If you are using RouterFunction, create a WebExceptionHandler bean to handle it manually.

@Bean
public WebExceptionHandler exceptionHandler() {
    return (ServerWebExchange exchange, Throwable ex) -> {
        if (ex instanceof PostNotFoundException) {
            exchange.getResponse().setStatusCode(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND);
            return exchange.getResponse().setComplete();
        }
        return Mono.error(ex);
    };
}

Note

WebExceptionHandler is a low-level API. It also works for the exception handling in the annotated controller case — the @ExceptionHandler mechanism itself is implemented as a chain of WebExceptionHandlers.

docs.title: Registering a WebExceptionHandler in Spring Boot
docs.text:
In a Spring Boot application, register the handler as a @Component with an explicit @Order(-2) so it runs before the default ErrorWebExceptionHandler (which has order -1):

@Component
@Order(-2)
class RestWebExceptionHandler implements WebExceptionHandler {

    @Override
    public Mono<Void> handle(ServerWebExchange exchange, Throwable ex) {
        if (ex instanceof PostNotFoundException) {
            exchange.getResponse().setStatusCode(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND);

            // marks the response as complete and forbids writing to it
            return exchange.getResponse().setComplete();
        }
        return Mono.error(ex);
    }
}

For the complete codes, check spring-reactive-sample/exception-handler and spring-reactive-sample/boot-exception-handler.

docs.title: RouterFunction
docs.text:
Functional routing provides a concise, fluent alternative to @RestController. Introduced in the Spring 5 era, RouterFunction remains fully supported in Spring Framework 7. It lets you compose routes and handlers using a functional API instead of controller classes.

For example, there is a simple controller class.

@RestController
@RequestMapping
class MessageController {

    @GetMapping
    Flux<Message> allMessages(){
        return Flux.just(
            Message.builder().body("hello Spring Framework 7").build(),
            Message.builder().body("hello Spring Boot 4").build()
        );
    }

}

You can write the same functionality with a RouterFunction bean instead.

@Bean
public RouterFunction<ServerResponse> routes() {
    return route(GET("/"),(ServerRequest req)-> ok()
                 .body(
                     BodyInserters.fromValue(
                         Arrays.asList(
                             Message.builder().body("hello Spring Framework 7").build(),
                             Message.builder().body("hello Spring Boot 4").build()
                         )
                     )
                 )
                );
}

The route (from RouterFunctions) accepts a RequestPredicate and a HandlerFunction. HandlerFunction is a @FunctionalInterface.

RouterFunctions and RequestPredicates are helpers to make it easy to assemble the request routes and predicates.

@FunctionalInterface
public interface HandlerFunction<T extends ServerResponse> {
    Mono<T> handle(ServerRequest var1);
}

You can extract the handler codes into a new class.

The following code fragments demonstrates the same features of PostController but written in RouterFunction.

@Bean
public RouterFunction<ServerResponse> routes(PostHandler postController) {
    return route(GET("/posts"), postController::all)
        .andRoute(POST("/posts"), postController::create)
        .andRoute(GET("/posts/{id}"), postController::get)
        .andRoute(PUT("/posts/{id}"), postController::update)
        .andRoute(DELETE("/posts/{id}"), postController::delete);
}

The implementations of HandlerFunction are centralized in a PostHandler class.

@Component
class PostHandler {

    private final PostRepository posts;

    public PostHandler(PostRepository posts) {
        this.posts = posts;
    }

    public Mono<ServerResponse> all(ServerRequest req) {
        return ServerResponse.ok().body(this.posts.findAll(), Post.class);
    }

    public Mono<ServerResponse> create(ServerRequest req) {
        return req.bodyToMono(Post.class)
            .flatMap(post -> this.posts.save(post))
            .flatMap(p -> ServerResponse.created(URI.create("/posts/" + p.getId())).build());
    }

    public Mono<ServerResponse> get(ServerRequest req) {
        return this.posts.findById(req.pathVariable("id"))
            .flatMap(post -> ServerResponse.ok().body(Mono.just(post), Post.class))
            .switchIfEmpty(ServerResponse.notFound().build());
    }

    public Mono<ServerResponse> update(ServerRequest req) {

        return Mono
            .zip(
                (data) -> {
                    Post p = (Post) data[0];
                    Post p2 = (Post) data[1];
                    p.setTitle(p2.getTitle());
                    p.setContent(p2.getContent());
                    return p;
                },
                this.posts.findById(req.pathVariable("id")),
                req.bodyToMono(Post.class)
            )
            .cast(Post.class)
            .flatMap(post -> this.posts.save(post))
            .flatMap(post -> ServerResponse.noContent().build());

    }

    public Mono<ServerResponse> delete(ServerRequest req) {
        return ServerResponse.noContent().build(this.posts.deleteById(req.pathVariable("id")));
    }

}

Note

The RouterFunction is ported back to the Servlet stack since Spring Framework 5.2 — check my example hantsy/spring-webmvc-functional-sample.

docs.title: An introduction to Reactive Web
docs.text:
Unlike the traditional Servlet stack, the Reactive Web stack introduced in Spring Framework 5 was rewritten from scratch using the Reactive Streams specification and the Reactor API.

There are two important abstractions in the Reactive Web stack that handle a web request.

  • WebHandler — the high-level API that assembles the resources such as WebFilter, ExceptionHandler, and so on to handle web requests from a client.
  • HttpHandler — the low-level API that adapts web handlers to the underlying runtime environment, such as Netty, as well as Servlet containers which provide async capability.

You can review the Application class in the Getting Started chapter to see both abstractions wired together:

HttpHandler handler = WebHttpHandlerBuilder.applicationContext(context).build();
ReactorHttpHandlerAdapter adapter = new ReactorHttpHandlerAdapter(handler);
HttpServer httpServer = HttpServer.create().host("localhost").port(this.port);
return httpServer.handle(adapter);

Base projects for this chapter

The examples in this chapter extend the two applications assembled in Getting Started: the vanilla application (manual wiring, no Spring Boot) and the Spring Boot application (spring-boot-starter-webflux). Each page names the sample in the repository that holds the complete code.

docs.title: Enabling WebFlux
docs.text:
To activate Reactive Web, create a @Configuration class and add an @EnableWebFlux annotation to enable WebFlux support.

@Configuration
@EnableWebFlux
class WebConfig {}

Similar to the existing WebMvcConfigurer in the Servlet stack, there is a WebFluxConfigurer interface for you to customize the details of web resources, validation, CORS, and so on.

You can create a configuration class to derive this interface and override the methods to customize the built-in configuration.

@Configuration
@EnableWebFlux
class WebConfig implements WebFluxConfigurer {}

Note

For Spring Boot applications, no extra steps are required to activate WebFlux if spring-boot-starter-webflux is included in the classpath.

docs.title: RxJava 3
docs.text:
By default, Spring WebFlux heavily depends on Reactor, but it also supports RxJava 3 APIs via adapters.

To use RxJava APIs instead of Reactor's API, firstly add RxJava in project dependencies.

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.reactivex.rxjava3</groupId>
    <artifactId>rxjava</artifactId>
</dependency>

Then you can use RxJava API freely in the @RestController like the APIs in the reactive Repository.

@RestController
@RequestMapping(value = "/posts")
class PostController {

    private final PostRepository posts;

    public PostController(PostRepository posts) {
        this.posts = posts;
    }

    @GetMapping(value = "")
    public Observable<Post> all() {
        return this.posts.findAll();
    }

    @GetMapping(value = "/{id}")
    public Maybe<Post> get(@PathVariable(value = "id") UUID id) {
        return this.posts.findById(id);
    }

    @PostMapping(value = "")
    public Single<Post> create(Post post) {
        return this.posts.save(post);
    }
}

For the complete codes, check spring-reactive-sample/rxjava3.

docs.title: The JDK Flow API
docs.text:
The java.util.concurrent.Flow API packages the Reactive Streams interfaces inside the JDK. Spring WebFlux provides adapter support for it, so you can use Flow.Publisher as a controller method return type or parameter.

@RestController
@RequestMapping(value = "/posts")
public class PostController {

    @GetMapping
    public Flow.Publisher<Post> all() {
        return JdkFlowAdapter.publisherToFlowPublisher(
                Flux.just(
                        new Post(1L, "post one", "content of post one"),
                        new Post(2L, "post two", "content of post two")
                )
        );
    }

}

docs.title: SmallRye Mutiny
docs.text:
SmallRye Mutiny support is added in Spring Framework 5.3.10. For developers, you can use Mutiny APIs instead of Reactor to build Spring WebFlux applications.

            <version>3.1.0</version>
            <type>pom</type>
            <scope>import</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

<dependencies>

    <dependency>
        <groupId>io.smallrye.reactive</groupId>
        <artifactId>mutiny</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    ...

</dependencies>

class PostController {

        this.posts = posts;
    }

    @GetMapping(value = "")
    public Multi<Post> all() {

    }

        return this.posts.save(post).map(p -> ResponseEntity.created(URI.create("/posts/" + p.getId())).build());
    }

}

docs.title: Multipart Support
docs.text:
In Spring, the Servlet stack supports multipart requests through the Servlet 3.0+ built-in multipart feature or Apache Commons IO. The WebFlux stack also adds multipart support — backed by non-blocking stream processing instead of buffering whole files in memory.

The Part abstraction represents a part in a multipart/form-data request. A part is either a FilePart (uploaded file content) or a FormFieldPart (a simple form field), whether the request comes from a browser form or any other client.

docs.title: Reading parts in a controller
docs.text:
The reactive controllers accept Part parameters wrapped in Mono or Flux. The following variants are supported:

@PostMapping("/requestBodyMap")
Mono<String> requestBodyMap(
    @RequestPart("fileParts") FilePart fileParts,
    @RequestPart("fileParts") Mono<FilePart> filePartsMono,
    @RequestPart("fileParts") Flux<FilePart> filePartsFlux,
    @RequestBody Mono<MultiValueMap<String, Part>> partsMono) {
    // ...
}

For a streaming approach, consume all parts as a Flux<Part> — this is the variant the sample implements:

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/uploads")
public class MultipartController {

    @PostMapping(value = "", consumes = MediaType.MULTIPART_FORM_DATA_VALUE)
    Mono<String> requestBodyFlux(@RequestBody Flux<Part> parts) {
        return partFluxDescription(parts);
    }

    private static Mono<String> partFluxDescription(Flux<? extends Part> partsFlux) {
        return partsFlux.log().collectList().map(MultipartController::partListDescription);
    }

    private static String partDescription(Part part) {
        return part instanceof FilePart fp ? part.name() + ":" + fp.filename() : part.name();
    }

    // partListDescription(...) joins the part descriptions into a single string
}

For the complete codes, check spring-reactive-sample/multipart.

docs.title: Streaming with PartEvent
docs.text:
Beyond the aggregated forms above, WebFlux can consume a multipart request as a stream of PartEvent messages — one event per form field and a pair of events (start/content) per file part. This processes parts as they arrive instead of buffering them, and scales to large uploads.

From the multipart sample of the spring6-sandbox repository, the controller consumes Flux<PartEvent>, splits the stream at each part boundary with windowUntil(PartEvent::isLast), and dispatches on the event type:

@PostMapping("partevents")
public ResponseEntity<Flux<String>> handlePartsEvents(@RequestBody Flux<PartEvent> allPartsEvents) {
    var result = allPartsEvents
            .windowUntil(PartEvent::isLast)
            .concatMap(p -> {
                        return p.switchOnFirst((signal, partEvents) -> {
                                    if (signal.hasValue()) {
                                        PartEvent event = signal.get();
                                        if (event instanceof FormPartEvent formEvent) {
                                            String value = formEvent.value();
                                            // handle form field
                                            log.debug("form value: {}", value);
                                            return Mono.just(value + "
");

                                        } else if (event instanceof FilePartEvent fileEvent) {
                                            String filename = fileEvent.filename();
                                            log.debug("upload file name:{}", filename);

                                            return partEvents.map(PartEvent::content)
                                                    .map(DataBufferUtils::release)
                                                    .then(Mono.just(filename + "
"));
                                        }

                                        return Mono.error(new RuntimeException("Unexpected event: " + event));
                                    }
                                    return Flux.empty(); // either complete or error signal
                                }
                        );
                    }
            );

    return ok().body(result);
}

Reading the flow:

  1. windowUntil(PartEvent::isLast) groups the event stream into windows, one per part.
  2. switchOnFirst inspects the first event of each window: a FormPartEvent carries the field value directly, a FilePartEvent opens the file — the content events that follow stream the file data (partEvents.map(PartEvent::content)), where you would write to storage instead of releasing the buffers.
  3. DataBufferUtils::release frees the buffer memory once the content is consumed.

The controller also demonstrates the other multipart consumption styles — a form command object, @RequestPart parameters, and Mono<MultiValueMap<String, Part>>:

@PostMapping("form")
public ResponseEntity handleFileUploadForm(FileUploadCommand form, BindingResult errors) {
    var result = Map.of(
            "name", form.getName(),
            "filename", form.getFile().filename()
    );
    return ok().body(result);
}

@PostMapping("requestparts")
public ResponseEntity handleRequestParts(@RequestPart("name") String name,
                                         @RequestPart("file") FilePart file) {
    var result = Map.of(
            "name", name,
            "filename", file.filename()
    );
    return ok().body(result);
}

@PostMapping("multivalues")
public ResponseEntity handleMultivalues(@RequestBody Mono<MultiValueMap<String, Part>> parts) {
    var partNames = parts.map(p -> p.keySet().stream().map(key -> p.getFirst(key).name()).toList()).log();
    return ok().body(partNames);
}

A test builds the PartEvent stream on the client side with FormPartEvent.create(...) and FilePartEvent.create(...):

@Test
public void testHandlePartEvents() {
    this.client
            .post().uri("/partevents")
            .contentType(MULTIPART_FORM_DATA)
            .body(
                    Flux.concat(
                            FormPartEvent.create("name", "test"),
                            FilePartEvent.create("file", new ClassPathResource("spring.png"))
                    ),
                    PartEvent.class
            )
            .exchange()
            .expectStatus().isOk()
            .expectBodyList(String.class).hasSize(2);
}

For the complete codes, check the multipart module of the spring6-sandbox repository.

docs.title: File upload and download
docs.text: For file upload/download backed by a store, stream the FilePart content into the backend of your choice. The Mongo GridFS example stores uploads in MongoDB via ReactiveGridFsTemplate and streams them back on download; the R2DBC FilePart example maps upload content to Postgres bytea (byte[], ByteBuffer, or R2DBC Blob).

docs.title: Server Sent Events
docs.text:
SSE (Server Sent Events) provides one-way server-to-client communication over the existing HTTP protocol. In real world applications, it is useful for sending notifications to clients or pushing near real-time updates in a stream — news feeds, stock prices, or chat updates.

In WebFlux, an SSE endpoint is a controller method (or a functional route) that produces a Flux with the text/event-stream content type. The stream can come from anywhere — a timer, a database tailable cursor, or a Sinks hub that broadcasts messages as they arrive.

docs.title: Emitting a stream from a timer
docs.text:
Set the content type to text/event-stream and return a Flux. The following example emits a time-paced event:

@GetMapping(produces = MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE)
public Flux<Post> sse() {
    return Flux
        .zip(Flux.interval(Duration.ofSeconds(1)), this.posts.findAll().repeat())
        .map(Tuple2::getT2);
}

docs.title: Broadcasting with Sinks
docs.text:
For an application where clients push messages and all connected clients receive them, a Reactor Sinks.Many acts as a hub: the service exposes the sink as a Flux for subscribers, and pushes new messages into it as they arrive.

@Service
public class MessageService {

    private final Sinks.Many<Message> sinks = Sinks.many().replay().latest();

    public Flux<Message> latestMessages() {
        return sinks.asFlux();
    }

    public void send(Message m) {
        sinks.emitNext(m, EmitFailureHandler.FAIL_FAST);
    }

}

The replay().latest() configuration replays the most recent message to a new subscriber, so a client reconnecting to the stream sees the latest state.

Expose the stream with a controller:

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/messages")
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class MessageController {

    private final MessageService messageService;

    @GetMapping(value = "", produces = MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE)
    public Flux<Message> messageStream() {
        return this.messageService.latestMessages();
    }

    @PostMapping(value = "", consumes = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)
    public Mono<ResponseEntity<?>> send(@RequestBody MessageRequest request) {
        var message = Message.builder()
            .id(UUID.randomUUID())
            .body(request.message())
            .sentAt(LocalDateTime.now())
            .build();
        this.messageService.send(message);
        return Mono.just(created(URI.create("/messages/" + message.getId())).build());
    }
}

Every POST /messages fans out to all SSE subscribers of GET /messages.

docs.title: Client side
docs.text:
There is no special client for SSE. Like interacting with RESTful APIs, use the existing WebClient to consume an SSE endpoint, and set the Accept header to text/event-stream:

client.get()
    .uri("messages")
    .accept(MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM)
    .retrieve()
    .bodyToFlux(Message.class)
    .subscribe(System.out::println);

In a browser, the built-in EventSource API consumes the same endpoint.

For a complete real world application, see hantsy/angular-spring-sse-sample, in which the client is built with Angular and the server side is a simple Spring Boot application that uses SSE to broadcast chat messages — backed by a MongoDB tailable cursor, see Tailable Query.

docs.title: View and View Resolvers
docs.text: Like the traditional Spring MVC, Spring WebFlux also includes the capability to rendering views by the integrated template engine.

docs.title: Thymeleaf
docs.text:
Thymeleaf is the most popular template engine in the Spring ecosystem.

Add the Thymeleaf Spring integration artifact that matches your Spring Framework version:

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.thymeleaf</groupId>
    <artifactId>thymeleaf-spring6</artifactId>
</dependency>

Configure Thymeleaf in a Spring web application.

@Configuration
@EnableWebFlux
class WebConfig implements ApplicationContextAware, WebFluxConfigurer {

    private ApplicationContext ctx;

    @Override
    public void setApplicationContext(ApplicationContext context) {
        this.ctx = context;
    }

    @Bean
    public SpringResourceTemplateResolver thymeleafTemplateResolver() {

        final SpringResourceTemplateResolver resolver = new SpringResourceTemplateResolver();
        resolver.setApplicationContext(this.ctx);
        resolver.setPrefix("classpath:/templates/");
        resolver.setSuffix(".html");
        resolver.setTemplateMode(TemplateMode.HTML);
        resolver.setCacheable(false);
        resolver.setCheckExistence(false);
        return resolver;

    }

    @Bean
    public ISpringWebFluxTemplateEngine thymeleafTemplateEngine() {
        // We override here the SpringTemplateEngine instance that would otherwise be
        // instantiated by
        // Spring Boot because we want to apply the SpringWebFlux-specific context
        // factory, link builder...
        final SpringWebFluxTemplateEngine templateEngine = new SpringWebFluxTemplateEngine();
        templateEngine.setTemplateResolver(thymeleafTemplateResolver());
        return templateEngine;
    }

    @Bean
    public ThymeleafReactiveViewResolver thymeleafChunkedAndDataDrivenViewResolver() {
        final ThymeleafReactiveViewResolver viewResolver = new ThymeleafReactiveViewResolver();
        viewResolver.setTemplateEngine(thymeleafTemplateEngine());
//        viewResolver.setOrder(1);
//        viewResolver.setViewNames(new String[]{"home"});
        viewResolver.setResponseMaxChunkSizeBytes(8192); // OUTPUT BUFFER size limit
        return viewResolver;
    }

    @Override
    public void configureViewResolvers(ViewResolverRegistry registry) {
        registry.viewResolver(thymeleafChunkedAndDataDrivenViewResolver());
    }

}

Thymeleaf provides reactive support in the template engine and allow you render a Flux stream dynamically.

An example of Thymeleaf template.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
  <head>
    <title>Simple Blog Posts</title>
    <meta charset="UTF-8" />
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0" />
  </head>
  <body>
    <h1>All posts</h1>
    <div>
      <table>
        <thead>
          <tr>
            <th>ID</th>
            <th>Title</th>
            <th>Content</th>
          </tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
          <tr th:each="e : ${posts}">
            <td th:text="${e.id}"></td>
            <td th:text="${e.title}"></td>
            <td th:text="${e.content}"></td>
          </tr>
        </tbody>
      </table>
    </div>
  </body>
</html>

docs.title: Freemarker
docs.text:
Spring Framework 7 provides built-in support for the Freemarker template engine in WebFlux.

Add Freemarker dependencies.

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.freemarker</groupId>
    <artifactId>freemarker</artifactId>
</dependency>

Add Freemarker configuration.

@Configuration
@EnableWebFlux
class WebConfig implements ApplicationContextAware, WebFluxConfigurer {

    private ApplicationContext ctx;

    @Override
    public void setApplicationContext(ApplicationContext context) {
        this.ctx = context;
    }

    @Bean
    public FreeMarkerConfigurer freeMarkerConfig() {
        Map<String, Object> variables = new HashMap<>();
        variables.put("xml_escape", new XmlEscape());

        FreeMarkerConfigurer configurer = new FreeMarkerConfigurer();
        configurer.setPreferFileSystemAccess(false);
        configurer.setTemplateLoaderPath("classpath:/templates");
        configurer.setResourceLoader(this.ctx);
        configurer.setFreemarkerVariables(variables);

        return configurer;
    }

    @Override
    public void configureViewResolvers(ViewResolverRegistry registry) {
        registry.freeMarker();
    }

}

An example of Freemarker template.

<html>
    <head>
        <title>Simple Blog Posts</title>
        <meta charset="UTF-8"/>
        <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0"/>
    </head>
    <body>

            <table>
                <thead>
                    <tr>
                        <th> ID</th>

                        <th>Content</th>
                    </tr>

                <tbody>

                        <#list posts as post>
                        <tr>
                            <td>${post.id}</td>

                        nothing

docs.title: Mustache
docs.text:
Mustache is a popular template engine in the Ruby and NodeJS world, it also provides Java implementation.

Spring framework does not integrate Mustache as Freemarker. But you can create your own Veiw and ViewResolver to adapt the Mustache compiler to the Spring world.

Add Mustache java into dependencies, we use jmustache here.

<dependency>
    <groupId>com.samskivert</groupId>
    <artifactId>jmustache</artifactId>
</dependency>

Then create a MustacheView to render the tempalte.

public class MustacheView extends AbstractUrlBasedView {

    private Compiler compiler;

    private String charset;

    /**
     * Set the JMustache compiler to be used by this view. Typically this property is not
     * set directly. Instead a single {@link Compiler} is expected in the Spring
     * application context which is used to compile Mustache templates.
     * @param compiler the Mustache compiler
     */
    public void setCompiler(Compiler compiler) {
        this.compiler = compiler;
    }

    /**
     * Set the charset used for reading Mustache template files.
     * @param charset the charset to use for reading template files
     */
    public void setCharset(String charset) {
        this.charset = charset;
    }

    @Override
    public boolean checkResourceExists(Locale locale) throws Exception {
        return resolveResource() != null;
    }

    @Override
    protected Mono<Void> renderInternal(Map<String, Object> model, MediaType contentType,
                                        ServerWebExchange exchange) {
        Resource resource = resolveResource();
        if (resource == null) {
            return Mono.error(new IllegalStateException(
                    "Could not find Mustache template with URL [" + getUrl() + "]"));
        }
        DataBuffer dataBuffer = exchange.getResponse().bufferFactory().allocateBuffer();
        try (Reader reader = getReader(resource)) {
            Template template = this.compiler.compile(reader);
            Charset charset = getCharset(contentType).orElse(getDefaultCharset());
            try (Writer writer = new OutputStreamWriter(dataBuffer.asOutputStream(),
                    charset)) {
                template.execute(model, writer);
                writer.flush();
            }
        }
        catch (Exception ex) {
            DataBufferUtils.release(dataBuffer);
            return Mono.error(ex);
        }
        return exchange.getResponse().writeWith(Flux.just(dataBuffer));
    }

    private Resource resolveResource() {
        Resource resource = getApplicationContext().getResource(getUrl());
        if (resource == null || !resource.exists()) {
            return null;
        }
        return resource;
    }

    private Reader getReader(Resource resource) throws IOException {
        if (this.charset != null) {
            return new InputStreamReader(resource.getInputStream(), this.charset);
        }
        return new InputStreamReader(resource.getInputStream());
    }

    private Optional<Charset> getCharset(MediaType mediaType) {
        return Optional.ofNullable(mediaType != null ? mediaType.getCharset() : null);
    }

}

Create a MustacheViewResolver to resolve a view.

public class MustacheViewResolver extends UrlBasedViewResolver {

    private final Compiler compiler;

    private String charset;

    /**
     * Create a {@code MustacheViewResolver} backed by a default instance of a
     * {@link Compiler}.
     */
    public MustacheViewResolver() {
        this.compiler = Mustache.compiler();
        setViewClass(requiredViewClass());
    }

    /**
     * Create a {@code MustacheViewResolver} backed by a custom instance of a
     * {@link Compiler}.
     *
     * @param compiler the Mustache compiler used to compile templates
     */
    public MustacheViewResolver(Compiler compiler) {
        this.compiler = compiler;
        setViewClass(requiredViewClass());
    }

    /**
     * Set the charset.
     *
     * @param charset the charset
     */
    public void setCharset(String charset) {
        this.charset = charset;
    }

    @Override
    protected Class<?> requiredViewClass() {
        return MustacheView.class;
    }

    @Override
    protected AbstractUrlBasedView createView(String viewName) {
        MustacheView view = (MustacheView) super.createView(viewName);
        view.setCompiler(this.compiler);
        view.setCharset(this.charset);
        return view;
    }

}

Configure MustacheViewResolver .

@Configuration
@EnableWebFlux
class WebConfig implements ApplicationContextAware, WebFluxConfigurer {

    private ApplicationContext ctx;

    @Override
    public void setApplicationContext(ApplicationContext context) {
        this.ctx = context;
    }

    @Bean
    public ViewResolver mustacheViewResolver() {
        String prefix = "classpath:/templates/";
        String suffix = ".mustache";
        Mustache.TemplateLoader loader = new MustacheResourceTemplateLoader(prefix, suffix);
        MustacheViewResolver mustacheViewResolver = new MustacheViewResolver(Mustache.compiler().withLoader(loader));
        mustacheViewResolver.setPrefix(prefix);
        mustacheViewResolver.setSuffix(suffix);
        return mustacheViewResolver;
    }

    @Override
    public void configureViewResolvers(ViewResolverRegistry registry) {
        registry.viewResolver(mustacheViewResolver());
    }

}

The MustacheResourceTemplateLoader is a Spring aware template resource loader.

public class MustacheResourceTemplateLoader implements TemplateLoader, ResourceLoaderAware {

    private String suffix = "classpath:templates/";
    private String prefix = ".mustache";
    private String charset = "UTF-8";

    private ResourceLoader resourceLoader = new DefaultResourceLoader();

    public MustacheResourceTemplateLoader(String prefix, String suffix) {
        this.prefix = prefix;
        this.suffix = suffix;
    }

    /**
     * Set the charset.
     *
     * @param charset the charset
     */
    public void setCharset(String charset) {
        this.charset = charset;
    }

    /**
     * Set the resource loader.
     *
     * @param resourceLoader the resource loader
     */
    @Override
    public void setResourceLoader(ResourceLoader resourceLoader) {
        this.resourceLoader = resourceLoader;
    }

    @Override
    public Reader getTemplate(String name) throws IOException {
        return new InputStreamReader(this.resourceLoader
                        .getResource(this.prefix + name + this.suffix).getInputStream(),
                this.charset);
    }

}

<section class="container">

    <div class="col-md-12">
      <div class="card">

          <h6 class="card-subtitle mb-2 text-muted">{{createdDate}}</h6>
          <p class="card-text">{{content}}</p>
          <a href="/posts/{{id}}" class="card-link">View Details</a>
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>
    {{/posts}}
  </div>
</section>
{{>footer}}

docs.title: WebFilter
docs.text:
WebFilter is a core component in the reactive stack that intercepts and processes HTTP requests and responses.

The WebFilter interface looks like the following.

public interface WebFilter {

    Mono<Void> filter(ServerWebExchange exchange, WebFilterChain chain);

}

The filter method receives a ServerWebExchange that lets you inspect the request and perform cross-cutting operations before or after the request is handled.

The WebFilterChain is similar to the role of FilterChain in the Servlet Filter. At runtime, a series of WebFilter can be chained to execute in one web request.

The following is an example of WebFilter where it works as a security checker. If there is no user query parameter provided, then send a UNAUTHORIZED status code to the response.

@Component
public class SecurityWebFilter implements WebFilter{
    @Override
    public Mono<Void> filter(ServerWebExchange exchange, WebFilterChain chain) {
        if(!exchange.getRequest().getQueryParams().containsKey("user")){
            exchange.getResponse().setStatusCode(HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED);
        }
        return chain.filter(exchange);
    }
}

Note

In production applications prefer Spring Security for authentication and authorization. This example demonstrates how a simple WebFilter can be used for small checks or prototyping.

For the complete codes, check spring-reactive-sample/web-filter.

docs.title: WebSocket
docs.text:
WebSocket is a bi-directional, multiplexed protocol built on HTTP. It is widely used for real-time client-server communication — chat, live updates, gaming — and supports custom subprotocols.

Spring WebFlux adds simple WebSocket support built on reactive types: a WebSocketHandler processes inbound and outbound streams of messages, and a HandlerMapping registers handlers at URLs.

docs.title: Step 1: implement a WebSocketHandler
docs.text:
Create a handler to process the incoming messages and send a response back to the client. The simplest form is an echo handler that loops the inbound stream back to the outbound stream:

public class EchoHandler implements WebSocketHandler {

    @Override
    public Mono<Void> handle(WebSocketSession session) {
        return session.send(session.receive()
                .doOnNext(WebSocketMessage::retain) // Use retain() for Reactor Netty
                .map(m -> session.textMessage("received:" + m.getPayloadAsText()))
        );
    }
}

WebSocketSession exposes receive() and send(Publisher<WebSocketMessage>) as reactive streams, so a handler is just a composition of the two flows.

A more realistic handler maintains a shared Sinks.Many and broadcasts every received message to all connected sessions — the same hub pattern as the SSE example:

@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class MessagetHandler implements WebSocketHandler {

    private final ObjectMapper objectMapper;

    private Sinks.Many<Message> sinks = Sinks.many().replay().limit(2);
    private Flux<Message> outputMessages = sinks.asFlux();
    private final ExecutorService executor = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor();

    @Override
    public Mono<Void> handle(WebSocketSession session) {
        var receiveMono = session.receive()
                .map(WebSocketMessage::getPayloadAsText)
                .map(this::readIncomingMessage)
                .flatMap(req -> Mono.fromCallable(
                        () -> new Message(UUID.randomUUID(), req.message(), LocalDateTime.now())))
                .log("server receiving::")
                .doOnNext(data -> executor.execute(
                        () -> sinks.emitNext(data, Sinks.EmitFailureHandler.FAIL_FAST)))
                .doOnError(error -> sinks.emitError(error, Sinks.EmitFailureHandler.FAIL_FAST))
                .then();

        var sendMono = session
                .send(
                        Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(500))
                                .thenMany(outputMessages.map(msg -> session.textMessage(toJsonString(msg)))))
                .log("server sending::")
                .onErrorResume(throwable -> session.close())
                .then();

        return Mono.zip(receiveMono, sendMono).then();
    }

    // toJsonString(...) and readIncomingMessage(...) convert to/from JSON
}

docs.title: Step 2: register the handler in a HandlerMapping
docs.text:
@Configuration
@EnableWebFlux
class WebConfig {

    @Bean
    public HandlerMapping handlerMapping(ObjectMapper objectMapper) {
        Map<String, WebSocketHandler> map = new HashMap<>();
        map.put("/echo", new EchoHandler());
        map.put("/ws/messages", new MessagetHandler(objectMapper));

        SimpleUrlHandlerMapping mapping = new SimpleUrlHandlerMapping();
        mapping.setUrlMap(map);
        return mapping;
    }

    @Bean
    WebSocketHandlerAdapter webSocketHandlerAdapter() {
        return new WebSocketHandlerAdapter();
    }
}

In a non-Spring Boot application, you have to declare the WebSocketHandlerAdapter bean explicitly. Spring Boot auto-configures it when spring-boot-starter-webflux is on the classpath.

docs.title: Client side
docs.text:
Spring provides a built-in Reactor Netty based WebSocket client to communicate with the server side.

The following test fragment connects to /echo, sends 100 messages, and collects the echoed responses:

WebSocketClient client = new ReactorNettyWebSocketClient();

int count = 100;
Flux<String> input = Flux.range(1, count).map(index -> "msg-" + index);
ReplayProcessor<Object> output = ReplayProcessor.create(count);

client.execute(new URI("ws://localhost:8080/echo"),
               session -> {
                   log.debug("Starting to send messages");
                   return session
                       .send(input.doOnNext(s -> log.debug("outbound " + s)).map(session::textMessage))
                       .thenMany(session.receive().take(count).map(WebSocketMessage::getPayloadAsText))
                       .subscribeWith(output)
                       .doOnNext(s -> log.debug("inbound " + s))
                       .then()
                       .doOnTerminate((aVoid, ex) ->
                               log.debug("Done with " + (ex != null ? ex.getMessage() : "success")));
               })
    .block(Duration.ofMillis(5000));
